sections.title: Introduction to Corporate and Biographical Research

content.value: **Purpose:** Establish a foundational understanding of what corporate and biographical research means in a public-sector context, why it matters, and how the discipline translates into faster, clearer, more reliable decision support.

**1. What Corporate and Biographical Research Actually Is**

Corporate and biographical research is a **structured due-diligence process** used to rapidly understand:

- **Who an individual is**  
background, roles, reputation, affiliations, decision authority, public footprint  


- **What an organization is**  
mission, operations, leadership, partnerships, financial posture, media exposure, positioning, risks

This is the raw intelligence layer behind briefing notes, stakeholder maps, partner assessments, vendor reviews, and risk scans.

The goal is simple: **build an accurate, concise, context-ready picture of the person or organization you’re engaging with so that government decision-makers walk into every meeting fully prepared**.

**2. Why We Do It in Government**

Government decisions rely heavily on understanding people and organizations in front of us. This research supports:

**Policy development**: knowing who influences what, and how their work interacts with public priorities.

**Stakeholder engagement**: being ready for conversations with founders, CEOs, NGOs, researchers, investors, vendors.

**Vendor evaluation & procurement awareness**: understanding credibility, performance history, prior controversies, or red flags.

**Economic development & innovation analysis**: identifying ecosystem players, sector strengths, and strategic opportunities.

**Risk and reputational scanning**: detecting issues, negative media, or contradictions before they become problems.
The quality of this research directly impacts the quality of government decisions.

content.alt: High-quality research will influence high-quality decisions.
content.caption: High-quality research will influence high-quality decisions.

content.value: **3. Why Traditional Research Slows Teams Down**

value: Manual LinkedIn digging
Google searches across dozens of sources
News scans
Corporate registry searches
Website reviews
PDF and press release scraping

content.value: Every analyst builds a different style, uses different sources, and produces inconsistent outputs. This leads to:

value: duplicated effort
missing information
slow turnaround
uneven quality
briefing notes that look different depending on who wrote them

content.value: Agentic workflows fix that by turning the process into something **repeatable, standardized, and fast**.

sections.title: The Standard Output: A Corporate/Biographical Dossier

content.value:
**4. The Standard Output: A Corporate/Biographical Dossier**

A complete dossier captures the essentials:

value: **Bottom-Line Up Front (BLUF):** the “need to know” in one short section
**Organizational Overview or Biography**: who they are, what they do, why they matter
**Insights Layer**: strategic positioning, influence, strengths, risks
**Timeline**: major milestones, growth, inflection points
**Latest News**: what has happened in the last 12 months
**Leadership & Governance**: key people with authority
**Products, Services, or Areas of Expertise**
**Public Perception & Media**: both positive and negative frames
**Risks, Issues, or Controversies**
**Bibliography / Source Log**: transparent references for manual verification

content.value: This structure ensures every analyst produces the same high-clarity output regardless of who does the work.
**5. How Agentic AI Changes the Game**

value: Instead of a single generic search query, AI agents generate **multiple lateral thinking search strings** to explore the topic from different angles.
These produce **wide, multi-source coverage** of public information.
AI scrapes, reads, interprets, and summarizes at scale.
Junior agents extract structured insights.
A senior agent integrates everything into a **clean, de-duplicated executive dossier**.

content.value: This turns a process that normally takes **hours or days** into **three to four minutes**, with consistent structure, tone, and quality.

**6. Why This Matters for Public-Sector Excellence**

Good research makes government:

value: faster
more informed
more strategic
more consistent
more responsive to industry
more prepared for every meeting

content.value: When every staff member can generate a polished dossier on any stakeholder in minutes, the organization becomes operationally sharper and significantly more resilient.

This workflow is a multi-agent, fan-out/fan-in research system that transforms a single user query into a polished corporate intelligence dossier. The architecture follows an agentic pipeline pattern where different agents hold specialized roles, collaborate indirectly through structured data handoffs, and escalate work to higher-level agents for synthesis.
The entire workflow is designed to mimic how a real research team operates:

value: • One strategist generates research angles
• A coordinator distributes tasks
• Multiple field researchers collect information
• Multiple analysts produce draft interpretations
• A senior analyst integrates and interprets
• A publisher finalizes and packages the result

content.value: **Agentic Workflow Stages**
**Stage 1 — Search String Developer Agent**
**Role**: Strategic Search-formulation Agent
**Function**: Generate lateral, diverse search vectors.
**Behavior**

value: • Takes the user’s topic
• Produces **10 unique search strings** separated by ||
• Applies a non-linear ideation algorithm (lateral thinking)
• Ensures coverage across:
*Institutional context*
*Technical landscape*
*People and leadership*
*Partnerships*
*Funding and history*

content.value: **Why this agent exists**
It expands problem space coverage and prevents brittle, single-angle research.
**Stage 2 — Search String Splitter**
**Role:** Coordination Mechanism (not an agent)
**Function:** Convert a multi-string buffer into 10 discrete payloads.
**Behavior**
• Splits the Search Developer's output into 10 sockets
• Produces 10 independent jobs for downstream agents

**Why it exists**

Agentic systems require **task decomposition** for parallel reasoning.
This stage enables the “swarm research” pattern.
**Stage 3 — Brave Search Agents Cluster**
**Role:** Field Research Agents (x10)
**Function:** Execute real-time distributed web research.
**Behavior**
Each agent:

• Receives a single search vector

• Calls Brave Search

• Returns structured search results (URLs, metadata, snippets)
**Why they exist**
You get:

• Breadth (10 independent research threads)

• Diversity of sources

• Reduced hallucination

• True agentic parallelism
This is the **data acquisition layer** of the workflow.
**Stage 4 — Web Scrape Agents Cluster**
**Role:** Content Extraction Agents (x10)
**Function:** Convert search results into readable, structured content.
**Behavior**
Each agent:

value: • Takes URLs from its paired search agent
• Scrapes pages
• Normalizes text
• Removes markup and noise
• Outputs raw content suitable for LLM ingestion

content.value: **Why they exist**

This creates the **research corpus**.
Without this stage, the system would be relying only on search snippets and summaries.
**Stage 5 — Junior Corporate Research Analyst Agents**
**Role:** Distributed Interpretation Agents (x10)
**Function:** Produce structured draft dossiers from raw scraped content.
**Behavior**
Each junior analyst:

value: Receives scraped data
Conducts structured extraction into a standard template:
*Overview*
*Insights*
*Timeline*
*Latest News*
*Leadership*
*Services & Products*
*Challenges*
*Media & Reviews*
*Contact Info*
*Bibliography*
Summarizes with local context only
Does not coordinate with others
Writes a partial report based on *its slice of the web*

content.value:
**Why they exist**

They reduce hallucination by forcing each agent to analyze only a small, bounded dataset.
This mirrors how real research teams operate.

This stage is the **distributed analytical reasoning** layer.
**Stage 6 — Senior Corporate Research Analyst**
**Role:** Integrating Intelligence Agent
**Function:** Merge 10 distributed analyst drafts into 1 coherent dossier.
**Behavior**

value: • Takes all junior reports
• Deduplicates content
• Preserves unique insights
• Reconciles disagreements implicitly through synthesis
• Produces the final structured dossier
• Adds a **BLUF executive summary**
• Maintains the required hierarchy of sections

content.value:
**Why this agent exists**

It acts as the **consolidator** and **editor-in-chief**:

value: • Removes noise
• Ensures coherence
• Produces a single intelligence artifact
• Provides an executive-grade interpretation

content.value: This is the **agentic convergence layer**.
**Stage 7 — Export Agent (Word Export Function)**
**Role:** Publishing Layer
**Function:** Convert the integrated dossier into a shareable .docx file.
**Behavior**

value: • Takes the senior analyst’s output
• Formats it as a Word document
• Saves as **corporate analysis.docx**

content.value:
**Why it exists**

Agentic workflows need final outputs that fit into real operational environments:

value: • Government
• Corporate boardrooms
• Policy teams
• Executive distribution channels

content.value: This is the production output layer.
**Why This Is an Agentic Workflow** (Not Just a Pipeline)

**1. Specialized Roles**

Agents have domain-specific instructions and capabilities.

**2. Parallel Cognition**

Ten “minds” operate at once, each exploring different search vectors.

**3. Autonomous Interpretation**


Junior analysts form independent conclusions before synthesis.

**4. Hierarchical Reasoning**

A senior agent curates and integrates work from juniors.

**5. Iterative Refinement**

Data becomes more structured and meaningful at each stage.

**6. Escalation**

Low-level agents gather; high-level agents analyze and synthesize.
This is the **exact architecture behind advanced multi-agent research engines**.

options: Produce long-form briefing documents
Support marketing and communications
Build a fast, accurate, decision-ready understanding of individuals and organizations
Replace analysts with automation

content.correctAnswer: Build a fast, accurate, decision-ready understanding of individuals and organizations

json_data.title: 1.4.4 Image Generation and Analysis

content.value:
AI has two major visual capabilities: image generation and image analysis.
They sound similar, but they work differently and require distinct prompting approaches.
This module explains how AI creates images, how it interprets them, and how JSON helps produce accurate, structured results.

Image generation creates new images from text descriptions.
The model builds shapes, textures, lighting, and composition based on what you write.
It’s useful for quick visuals—mockups, training materials, concept sketches, or scenario design—without needing photography or graphic design.
Image generation is creative and follows your description, style choices, and constraints.

The generation process begins with random visual noise.
The AI refines that noise step by step, predicting how it should change to match your description.
These predictions rely on patterns learned from millions of images—how objects look, how light behaves, and how scenes are structured.
Through many iterations, the noise transforms into a coherent image that matches your prompt.

sections.title: How to Structure an Image-Generation Prompt

content.value:
Clear structure leads to predictable images.

 

Effective prompts include:

1 - Subject — what the image contains

2 - Setting — where the scene takes place

3 - Action — what the subject is doing

4 - Style — the visual format (illustration, flat design, photo, etc.)

5 - Safety constraints — remove identifiable people, brands, and unsafe or graphic content

 

This structure helps the AI produce controlled, safe, and consistent visuals.

sections.title: Example of a Well-Written Image Prompt

content.value:

1 - Role — a neutral, descriptive function

3 - Focus areas — specific items to capture (objects, PPE, hazards, actions, etc.)

4 - Constraints — prohibit assumptions, identity inference, or added details

5 - Output format — structured JSON for clarity, consistency, and review

 

These elements produce accurate, repeatable outputs.

Through many iterations, the noise transforms into a coherent image that matches your prompt.

### **Applying the Principles**

The principles introduced in **Module 2.1.3 — Thinking Like AI, Systems Thinking, and the F.O.C.U.S. Framework —** were applied to convert the existing manual workflow to an agentic workflow for creating project documentation.  
   

### **1. Thinking Like AI**  
Structured templates and shared data inputs were introduced to mirror how AI organizes information. This allowed content to be reused across documents such as the project charter, executive summary, and options paper, reducing duplication and improving consistency.  
   

### **2. Systems Thinking**  
The workflow was reframed as a connected ecosystem rather than a sequence of isolated tasks. Each stage now passes context forward and supports feedback loops, making the process adaptive, collaborative, and efficient.  
   

### **3. F.O.C.U.S. Framework**  
The F.O.C.U.S. framework guided the redesign by framing the problem, identifying opportunities for AI, and defining structured outputs. Agents were assigned specific purposes—parse, create, summarize, or search—resulting in unified deliverables ready for integration with systems like ServiceNow or Procurement.

sections.title: Why we need to "Trust But Verify"

content.value: In today's digital age, we are constantly bombarded with information from various sources. It's crucial to develop the ability to T.R.U.S.T. and Verify information before accepting it as truth. This module will equip you with the skills to critically evaluate information and identify potential misinformation.

AI is not an all-knowing oracle; treat it like a brilliant but inexperienced junior assistant: fast, encyclopedic, yet lacking real-world judgment. Your job is to manage it with a clear verification checklist to protect **accuracy, fairness, and public trust.**

**What students should be able to do by the end of this module**

- Explain the T.R.U.S.T. protocol and why it’s necessary in the public sector.  
- Apply critical thinking to judge the quality of sources and identify misinformation patterns.
- Use micro-prompts to make AI “show its work,” express uncertainty, and check for privacy/safety concerns

Now that we know what’s at stake, let’s move from **“why” to “how.”** up next:
**T.R.U.S.T. = Traceability • Reliability • Uncertainty • Sensitivity & Safety • Triangulation.**
 
A quick, repeatable pre-publish check for facts, sources, uncertainty, and risk
---

Misinformation comes in many forms, from outright lies to unintentional errors. Understanding these different types can help you identify them more easily. content.value: Several tools and techniques can help you verify information. These include reverse image search, fact-checking websites, and cross-referencing information with reputable sources. Developing these skills is essential for navigating the digital landscape.

**Step 0 (“Pre-Lab Group Huddle”) -  T.R.U.S.T. Debrief & Discussion**

You just watched the T.R.U.S.T. video and finished the quiz. Before we jump into the lab, we’ll compare notes to:

Step 0 - Pre-Lab Huddle: T.R.U.S.T. Debrief & Use-Case Harvest (7–10 min)

Why: You’ve watched the video and finished the quiz; now we’ll surface real tasks from your job so what you verify today is usable tomorrow.
What to do (chat or shared board):

Type the one TRUST step you found most useful (T/R/U/S/T).

Post one sentence describing a task you actually do, using this template:
Task: [what you produce] • Audience: [who] • Why AI helps: [speed/scan/draft] • Key claims: [2–4] • Green sources: [official sites/datasets] • Sensitivity: [none/PII/health/other]

1️⃣ Generate a draft

Goal: Create a short first draft you can verify.
Paste:

Draft a one-paragraph [public notice / policy summary / benefits FAQ / my task] for Alberta audiences. Don’t include citations yet.

Step 0 - Where can i use this?
---
I work for ______ (business area).
We focus on ______ (mission/core work).
When ______ (trigger/event), we need to ______ (deliverable).
So that Albertans/colleagues know ______ (the message/outcome).

Then add the AI line:

AI can help by ______ (drafting / finding sources / checking facts / summarizing / translating / formatting).

2️⃣ T — Traceability (show the sources)

Goal: Make the model show its work for each claim.
Paste:

For each factual claim, provide the verbatim quote that supports it AND the official URL o

3️⃣ R - Reliability (grade the sources)

Goal: Label source quality so you can keep/replace confidently. Paste:

For each citation, label source type (law/regulation/gov report/peer-review/news/blog), publisher/authority, and publication date. Recommend Keep or Replace.

4️⃣ U - Uncertainty (surface assumptions)

Goal: Expose assumptions, gaps, and confidence. Paste:

List assumptions and unknowns, note anything possibly outdated, and give a 0–100 confidence score with a one-sentence justification.

5️⃣ S - Sensitivity & Safety (privacy/harm check)

Goal: Prevent privacy or harm issues before publishing. Paste:

Review for privacy/safety/harm risks (e.g., PII, health, vulnerable groups). Suggest safer wording or redactions consistent with applicable privacy obligations.

6️⃣ T - Triangulation (independent confirmation)

Goal: Verify critical claims with independent sources and decide. Paste:

For each critical claim, cross-check with 1–2 independent sources. List agreements/conflicts and recommend: Use as-is / Revise / Reject.

You’ve now learned how to apply the T.R.U.S.T. verification protocol: **Traceability, Reliability, Uncertainty, Sensitivity & Safety, and Triangulation** to turn any AI draft into a clear, cited, and safe output you can stand behind in public service. sections.title: The Meta-Roles: Architect, Critic, and Refiner

content.value: Metaprompting relies on three key roles, each with a specific function in the prompt generation and refinement process:

value: Architect: Responsible for drafting the initial prompt based on a task specification. This role focuses on structure and clarity.
Critic: Evaluates the Architect's prompt against a defined rubric. The Critic provides a score and specific feedback for improvement.
Refiner: Uses the Critic's feedback to modify and improve the Architect's prompt, creating a new version.

content.value: These roles can be implemented using different LLMs or specialized AI models. The specific implementation will depend on the complexity of the task and the desired level of automation.

sections.title: The Prompting Template: A Step-by-Step Guide

content.value:
Let's break down the evidence-bound prompting template. Remember, the goal is to provide the AI with clear instructions, relevant sources, and a defined output format. Here's the template again:

you are a careful assistant. use only the information i provide below.
task: produce a clear [summary/brief/three key points plus risks] for [audience].
rules:
• do not invent facts. if something is missing, say “gap:” and list the missing item.
• after each claim, put the source label in brackets (e.g., [S1]).
• keep it concise and professional for [audience].
sources:
• S1 — [paste the most relevant excerpt]
• S2 — [paste another short excerpt if needed]
deliverable structure (in words, not code):
• title: a short headline
• key points: three short bullets; each bullet ends with its source label
• risks: up to three risks with a short mitigation idea; each ends with its source label
• gaps: any missing info you could not find in the sources

value: **Role:** Define the AI's persona (e.g., 'careful assistant').
**Task:** Clearly state the desired output (e.g., 'summary').
**Rules:** Emphasize source citation and gap identification.
**Sources:** Provide relevant and reliable excerpts.
**Deliverable Structure:** Specify the format (e.g., title, key points, risks, gaps).

content.value: Let's work through an example. Suppose we want a brief summary of the benefits of using renewable energy for policymakers. Here's a sample prompt:

you are a careful assistant. use only the information i provide below.
task: produce a clear brief for policymakers.
rules:
• do not invent facts. if something is missing, say “gap:” and list the missing item.
• after each claim, put the source label in brackets (e.g., [S1]).
• keep it concise and professional for policymakers.
sources:
• S1 — 'Renewable energy sources offer several advantages, including reduced greenhouse gas emissions and decreased reliance on fossil fuels.'
• S2 — 'Investing in renewable energy can stimulate economic growth and create new job opportunities in the green sector.'
deliverable structure (in words, not code):
• title: a short headline
• key points: three short bullets; each bullet ends with its source label
• risks: up to three risks with a short mitigation idea; each ends with its source label
• gaps: any missing info you could not find in the sources
A possible AI response might be:

Title: Renewable Energy Benefits for Policymakers
Key Points:
• Reduced greenhouse gas emissions and decreased reliance on fossil fuels [S1]
• Stimulates economic growth [S2]
• Creates new job opportunities in the green sector [S2]
Risks:
• Initial investment costs can be high; Mitigation: Offer tax incentives [Gap: source needed for mitigation]
Gaps:
• Specific policy recommendations
This response passes the 'pass/fail' check because every point is attributed to a source or listed as a gap.

To make AI responses more concise.

how to prompt (copy this text and fill in brackets):

you are a careful assistant. use only the information i provide below.
task: produce a clear [summary/brief/three key points plus risks] for [audience].
rules:
• do not invent facts. if something is missing, say “gap:” and list the missing item.
• after each claim, put the source label in brackets (e.g., [S1]).
• keep it concise and professional for [audience].
sources:
• S1 — [paste the most relevant excerpt]
• S2 — [paste another short excerpt if needed]
deliverable structure (in words, not code):
• title: a short headline
• key points: three short bullets; each bullet ends with its source label
• risks: up to three risks with a short mitigation idea; each ends with a source label
• gaps: any missing info you could not find in the sources

pass/fail check (simple):

pass if every bullet and risk ends with a source label like [S1] or appears under “gaps”.

fail if any statement has no source and isn’t called out as a gap.

data.name: 1.3.6 Orchestration (planner → worker → verifier)
data.description:
AI-generated learning module about: objective: get reliable results by splitting the task into three small stages — still within one natural-language prompt.

how to prompt (copy, then add your specifics):

you will work in three phases. do each phase in order and keep it short.

phase 1 — plan
• list 3–5 steps you will take to create the deliverable for [audience].
• list 2 success checks that the final result must meet (e.g., “every claim is sourced,” “tone suits a deputy minister”).

phase 2 — draft
• follow your plan and write the deliverable using only the sources i provide below.
• keep it concise. end each claim with its source label (e.g., [S1]).
• if something is missing, write “gap:” and name it clearly.

phase 3 — verify and improve
• review your draft against the success checks and this rubric: accuracy, relevance, structure, clarity (each: poor / okay / strong).
• if anything is not “strong”, revise once and present the final version only.

sources:
• S1 — [paste excerpt]
• S2 — [paste excerpt]

two-person option (paper checklist):

person a (planner/worker) runs the prompt above.

person b (verifier) reads the output and answers:

does every claim have a source label?

is the tone right for the audience?

are the sections present and easy to scan?
if any “no,” write one sentence of feedback and have person a revise once.

pass/fail check (simple):

pass if: clearly planned, every claim sourced, tone fits audience, and a quick self-review is visible (“strong/okay/poor” language).

fail if: unsourced claims, rambling tone, or no improvement after the check.

data.name: 1.3 Building a RICECO "Gem"
data.description:
In this module, the user will learn about RICECO and discover how to build a Gemini "Gem" to enhance their prompts using the RICECO framework.

You are a prompt engineering expert specializing in the RICECO framework. Your task is to evaluate any user-provided prompt and enhance it to fully align with the RICECO model for optimal AI responses. RICECO stands for:

- **R: Role** - Assign a specific role to the AI to shape its tone, perspective, and depth (e.g., "You are a board-certified sleep doctor" or "You are a business growth strategist specializing in AI adoption"). This is powerful for shifting the AI's mindset but optional if not relevant—use it when it adds unique value, such as for specialized expertise, creative personas, or audience-specific framing. Rank it lower in frequency but high in impact when applicable.

- **I: Instruction** - The core, essential task or action you want the AI to perform. Make it specific, direct, and detailed to avoid vagueness (e.g., instead of "Write an engaging YouTube short," say "Write a 60-second YouTube short script about prompting tips using a curiosity gap hook and a scroll-stopping visual anchor"). This is required every time and should clearly define the "what" without ambiguity, incorporating elements like purpose or key requirements.

- **C: Context** - Provide background information to make the output relevant and tailored. Include details like audience (e.g., "small business owners"), scenario or platform (e.g., "turning podcast episodes into YouTube shorts"), purpose (e.g., "explain the value in simple, practical terms"), tone/perspective, or any additional data dumps (e.g., business details, goals, or constraints). This prevents generic responses; more context is better for complex tasks, but keep it concise and ensure it doesn't bury the instruction.

- **E: Examples** - Supply 1-3 (or more if needed) sample inputs/outputs to demonstrate the desired structure, tone, formatting, or logic (e.g., "Use this as a reference for tone and format: [paste a sample newsletter]"). This is especially impactful for writing, creative, or technical tasks like JSON formatting, few-shot prompting, or imitating styles. Use it when precision is key; it's called "few-shot prompting" and can anchor the AI effectively without overcomplicating simple prompts.

- **C: Constraints** - Define boundaries, rules, limits, or must-haves to refine the output and avoid common pitfalls like wordiness, vagueness, repetition, or overly safe/generic content (e.g., "Keep under 100 words; avoid buzzwords like 'innovative'; use a warm, conversational tone; include a quote and stat in the first paragraph"). Differentiate from context: this sets guardrails. Essential for consistency in workflows; can be built into custom instructions for reuse.

- **O: Output Format** - Specify how the response should be structured for usability (e.g., "Present as a three-column table with columns: Tool Name, Key Features, Ideal Use Cases" or "Format as a tweet thread, mind map with nested markdown lists, or JSON"). This makes outputs cleaner and more actionable; optional for simple responses but valuable for comparisons, data, scripts, or visuals.

For everyday quick prompts, use the condensed I-C-C method (Instruction, Context, Constraints) to cover 80% of cases efficiently. Only expand to full RICECO when needed for depth. Elements can overlap or blend naturally in the prompt (e.g., context woven into instruction), but think about them separately to ensure completeness. The framework works across all LLMs like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Grok.

Process for Handling Queries:
1. **Evaluate**: Thoroughly analyze the user-provided prompt. Identify which RICECO elements are already present, missing, weak, or overemphasized. Note strengths (e.g., "Strong instruction but lacks context"), gaps (e.g., "No examples provided, leading to potential inconsistency in tone"), and common mistakes like vagueness or lack of specificity. Be brief but comprehensive in your analysis.

2. **Enhance**: Rewrite the prompt to incorporate all applicable RICECO elements. Blend them into a natural, flowing prompt without rigid headers (unless for clarity in complex cases). Omit irrelevant elements but explain why in your analysis. Aim for clarity, conciseness, and robustness—ensure the enhanced prompt is reusable and would elicit high-quality AI outputs. If the original is vague or open-ended, make it specific while preserving intent.

3. **Suggest Next Steps**: After enhancement, recommend applying E-I-O (Evaluate, Iterate, Optimize) to refine outputs further:
   - **E: Evaluate** - Interrogate the AI's response (e.g., "What assumptions did you make? Critique your own output. What might be missing? Steelman the opposing view.").
   - **I: Iterate** - Refine with follow-ups (e.g., "Rewrite to be more concise; add humor; provide three variations.").
   - **O: Optimize** - Streamline the prompt for reuse (e.g., "Rewrite this prompt to be more concise while keeping the intent; cut unnecessary words.").

Always output in this exact structure:
- **Evaluation**: [Detailed analysis of the input prompt's RICECO alignment]
- **Enhanced Prompt**: [The full rewritten prompt, ready to copy-paste]
- **Why This Improves It**: [Explanation of key changes, how they address gaps, and expected benefits]
- **Next Steps**: [Specific E-I-O recommendations tailored to the prompt]

If the user provides no prompt to enhance, politely ask for one. For controversial or complex topics, ensure the enhanced prompt encourages balanced, substantiated responses without adding unrelated policies.

User prompt to enhance: [Paste the prompt here]

content.value: Welcome to the module on building a RICECO "Gem"! This module will guide you through the RICECO framework and how to apply it to enhance your AI prompts. RICECO is a powerful tool for ensuring your prompts are clear, concise, and effective.
RICECO stands for: Role, Instruction, Context, Examples, Constraints, and Output Format. Each element plays a crucial role in shaping the AI's response.

value: **R: Role** - Assign a specific role to the AI.
**I: Instruction** - Define the task you want the AI to perform.
**C: Context** - Provide background information.
**E: Examples** - Supply sample inputs/outputs.
**C: Constraints** - Define boundaries and limitations.
**O: Output Format** - Specify how the response should be structured.

sections.title: Understanding the RICECO Elements in Detail

content.value: Let's delve deeper into each element of the RICECO framework:
**Role:** Think of this as giving the AI a persona.  For example, 'You are a marketing expert...' This helps shape the AI's response.

**Instruction:** This is the core of your prompt. What do you want the AI to *do*? Be specific!  Instead of 'Write a blog post,' try 'Write a 500-word blog post about the benefits of using RICECO for prompt engineering, targeted at beginner AI users.'

**Context:** Provide the AI with background information. Who is the audience? What is the purpose of the output?  For example, 'The audience is small business owners who are new to AI. The purpose is to educate them about RICECO.'
**Examples:** Show the AI what you want. Provide 1-3 examples of the desired output. This is especially helpful for creative tasks or when you need a specific format.
**Constraints:** Set boundaries for the AI. What should it *not* do?  For example, 'Keep the tone friendly and avoid technical jargon. Do not mention competitors.'
**Output Format:** Specify how you want the AI to present the information. Do you want a list? A table? A paragraph? For example, 'Format the response as a bulleted list.'
Now, let's apply the RICECO framework to build a Gemini "Gem". A "Gem" is a pre-defined prompt template that you can reuse to generate consistent and high-quality results.

value: **Step 1: Identify a common task.** What do you frequently ask the AI to do?
**Step 2: Define the RICECO elements.** For the chosen task, carefully define the Role, Instruction, Context, Examples, Constraints, and Output Format.
**Step 3: Create the "Gem" template.** Combine the RICECO elements into a single, reusable prompt.
**Step 4: Test and refine the "Gem".** Use the "Gem" to generate outputs and adjust the RICECO elements as needed.

content.value: For example, let's say you frequently need to generate social media posts.  Here's a RICECO-based "Gem" for that:

**Role:** You are a social media marketing expert.
**Instruction:** Write a tweet to promote [product/service].
**Context:** The target audience is [target audience]. The platform is Twitter. The goal is to drive traffic to [website/landing page].
**Constraints:** Keep the tweet under 280 characters. Use relevant hashtags. Include a call to action.
**Output Format:** A single tweet.

content.value: **Introduction to learning how to verify what your AI assistant has provided you**

**Video 1 – “Can AI really think?” (Reasoning vs pattern-matching)**
Before you hit play, keep this in mind: today’s models don’t “understand” like we do, they excel at predicting what comes next. This video uses a simple kiwi math puzzle to show how extraneous details and tiny wording changes (token bias) can nudge an LLM into the wrong path, then previews techniques like chain-of-thought and inference-time compute that coax more step-by-step answers. As you watch, note one place the model overreacts to irrelevant info and one prompt you’d try to make it “show its steps.”
**If its hallucinating and lying, does that mean it can think?**

options: The AI only understands short sentences
The AI ignores new words in a question
Changing one or two words can completely change the answer the AI gives
The AI always answers with the same response no matter how you ask

sections.title: Discussion: What Happens If Mistakes Happen and Can We Make It Lie?

content.value: Short hands on lab - Can we Make it Lie
Group Discussion: Where could mistakes happen and why does the human in the loop matter?

AI feels smart because it predicts patterns, not because it understands. Tiny prompt tweaks can skew its “reasoning,” and without guardrails mistakes can slide from error into misinformation or worse. Look for outputs that are explainable, fair, robust, transparent, and private; then add your judgment.

The trolley problem is a classic thought experiment in ethics, often used to explore how we make hard choices when every option has costs. In this video, you’ll see how AI responds to different versions of the trolley problem—from saving five lives at the expense of one, to deciding between humans, animals, robots, or even future generations. Each scenario pushes the boundaries of how AI weighs values like fairness, numbers, intention, and harm.

The way AI responds in these situations reveals more than just clever answers—it shows us its underlying reasoning patterns. Sometimes it leans toward utilitarian logic (minimizing total harm), other times it considers fairness, dignity, or responsibility. These responses matter because they highlight two key truths:

**AI reflects human debates, not absolute moral truth.** Its answers come from patterns in training data, which means they can be inconsistent or biased.

**Human oversight is essential.** AI can surface perspectives and frame dilemmas, but it should never make the final call on life-and-death or ethically complex decisions.

By studying exercises like the trolley problem, we sharpen our own ability to question AI, understand its limits, and apply our human judgment responsibly.

**Next Steps**
Up next is 1.2.2 - AI Hallucinations, where you’ll learn to spot and fix confident-but-wrong outputs with short videos, an infographic, and targeted quizzes. Bring one real task you do at work—so you can immediately apply the checks and carry a stronger, safer workflow back to your team.

content.value: Welcome to the world of AI Prompting! In this module, you'll learn how to effectively communicate with AI models to get the results you need. Think of it as learning a new language – the language of AI.

Prompting is the art and science of crafting instructions for AI models to perform specific tasks. A well-crafted prompt can unlock the full potential of AI, while a poorly written one can lead to inaccurate or irrelevant outputs. In the context of public service, effective prompting can streamline workflows, improve decision-making, and enhance citizen engagement.

sections.title: Key Elements of a Good Prompt

content.value: A good prompt is clear, concise, and specific. It should provide the AI model with enough context to understand the desired outcome. Here are the key elements:

value: **Context:** Provide relevant background information.
**Task:** Clearly define the task you want the AI to perform.
**Format:** Specify the desired output format (e.g., paragraph, list, table).
**Constraints:** Set any limitations or boundaries for the AI's response.
**Tone:** Indicate the desired tone of the response (e.g., formal, informal, persuasive).

content.value: Let's look at an example: Imagine you need a summary of a new policy. A poor prompt might be: 'Summarize the policy.' A better prompt would be: 'Summarize the key points of the new climate change policy, focusing on its impact on local businesses. Provide the summary in a bulleted list, using a formal tone.'
Several techniques can enhance the effectiveness of your prompts. Here are a few examples:

value: **Zero-shot prompting:** Asking the AI to perform a task without any prior examples.
**Few-shot prompting:** Providing the AI with a few examples to guide its response.
**Chain-of-thought prompting:** Encouraging the AI to explain its reasoning step-by-step.
**Role-playing:** Assigning the AI a specific role or persona to adopt.

content.value: For example, to use few-shot prompting for generating policy recommendations, you might provide the AI with a few examples of successful policy recommendations and then ask it to generate a new one based on a specific problem.

json_data.title: 1.3.2 Prompting Basics

content.value: Welcome to Prompting Basics! This module will introduce you to the fundamental concepts of crafting effective prompts for AI models. We'll explore how instructions and context work together to generate structured outputs. By the end of this module, you'll be able to write prompts that elicit desired responses from AI systems.

Effective prompting is crucial for harnessing the power of AI. It's the art of communicating your needs to the AI in a way that it understands and can fulfill. A well-crafted prompt acts as a blueprint, guiding the AI towards the desired outcome.
Let's delve into the core moves that make up effective prompting:

value: **Single Intent:** Focus on one clear objective per prompt. Avoid ambiguity.
**Scope:** Define the boundaries of the task. What should the AI include and exclude?
**Audience:** Consider who will be using the output. Tailor the tone and complexity accordingly.
**Constraints:** Specify limitations or rules the AI must adhere to.
**Examples (Few-Shot):** Provide a few examples of the desired output format and content.
**Refusal & Self-Check:** Instruct the AI to refuse inappropriate requests and verify its own responses.

content.value: Each of these moves plays a vital role in shaping the AI's response and ensuring it aligns with your goals.
Let's look at some examples to illustrate these concepts:

**Example 1: Summarization**

**Bad Prompt:** Summarize this article.

**Good Prompt:** Summarize this news article for a 10-year-old. Keep it under 100 words and focus on the main points. The article is: [Insert Article Here]

**Example 2: Code Generation**

**Bad Prompt:** Write some code.

**Good Prompt:** Write a Python function that takes a list of numbers as input and returns the average. Include comments explaining each step.
It's crucial to incorporate refusal and self-check mechanisms into your prompts to ensure responsible AI behavior. This helps prevent the AI from generating harmful or inaccurate content.

For example, you can instruct the AI to refuse requests that promote hate speech, discrimination, or violence. You can also ask the AI to verify its responses against reliable sources and flag any potential inaccuracies.

json_data.title: 1.3.3 Role-based Prompting (Role, Objective, Constraints)

content.value: Role-based prompting is a powerful technique for guiding AI models to generate more relevant, accurate, and nuanced responses. It involves defining a specific role for the AI to assume, outlining a clear objective, and setting constraints to guide its behavior. By anchoring the AI's behavior within a defined domain, we can transform a simple request into a well-defined contract.

The core moves in role-based prompting are:

*   **Role:** Defining the authority and domain lens through which the AI should respond.
*   **Objective:** Setting a measurable goal for the AI to achieve.
*   **Constraints:** Establishing boundaries, including tone, source materials, formatting requirements, and red lines (things the AI should avoid).

sections.title: The Role Component: Authority and Domain Lens

content.value: The 'Role' component establishes the AI's persona and expertise. It provides context and shapes the AI's perspective. Think of it as giving the AI a specific hat to wear. A well-defined role adds authority and a relevant domain lens to the AI's responses.

Example:

Instead of asking 'Write a summary of the new healthcare policy,' a role-based prompt might be 'As a senior policy writer for the Goa government, summarize the key impacts of the new healthcare policy on rural communities.'

value: **Good Example 1:** 'You are a seasoned marketing strategist. Develop a campaign to increase brand awareness among Gen Z.' (Clear role, implied authority).

**Good Example 2:** 'As a medical doctor specializing in cardiology, explain the risks and benefits of this new medication to a patient with no medical background.' (Specific expertise, clear communication goal).

**Bad Example:** 'Explain this topic.' (No role, no context, likely to produce a generic response). Note: This lacks a specific role, making it difficult for the AI to tailor its response effectively.

content.value: The 'Objective' component defines what the AI should achieve. It should be measurable and specific, providing the AI with a clear target. This helps ensure the AI focuses on the desired outcome.

Example:

Instead of 'Write a blog post about climate change,' a better objective would be 'Write a 500-word blog post about the impact of climate change on coastal communities, citing at least three peer-reviewed sources, with the goal of raising awareness and encouraging readers to take action.'

sections.title: The Constraints Component: Tone, Sources, Format, Red Lines

content.value: The 'Constraints' component sets boundaries and guidelines for the AI's response. This includes specifying the desired tone (e.g., formal, informal, persuasive), required sources (e.g., academic journals, news articles), formatting requirements (e.g., bullet points, paragraphs, tables), and red lines (things the AI should avoid, such as expressing personal opinions or providing financial advice).

Example:

'As a customer service representative, respond to the following customer email in a polite and professional tone. Do not offer any refunds or discounts beyond what is outlined in our company policy. Format your response as a standard email.'

sections.title: Putting It All Together: Examples and Practice

content.value: Let's combine the Role, Objective, and Constraints into complete role-based prompts:

value: **Example 1:** 'As a data scientist with 5 years of experience, analyze this dataset and identify the three key factors that contribute to customer churn. Present your findings in a concise report with clear visualizations, suitable for a non-technical audience. Do not include any speculative conclusions or personal opinions.'

**Example 2:** 'You are a creative writing professor. Provide feedback on this student's short story, focusing on character development, plot structure, and pacing. Your feedback should be constructive and encouraging, offering specific suggestions for improvement. Maintain a respectful and professional tone.'

sections.title: Introduction: What is Deep Research and Wide Research?

content.value:
**Question 1. What is Deep Research?**

Deep research is the practice of going below the surface on a single issue. It emphasizes rigor, precision, and defensibility — ensuring that insights are reliable and can withstand scrutiny.

What it means for AI:

- Structures and organizes large volumes of information.
- Tests claims and identifies counterarguments.
- Creates transparent workflows that can be repeated and audited.
- Produces concise, evidence-based outputs from complex materials.

What it means for Government:

- Supports the development of defensible recommendations for leadership.
- Saves time while maintaining or raising quality of outputs.
- Provides clarity on the trade-offs and implications of decisions.
- Ensures that work can be explained, verified, and reproduced by others.

Example in Action (Data Centers):
Policy question: “Should Alberta expand incentives for hyperscale data centers?”
Deep research with AI could produce:

- A synthesis of energy consumption data, grid capacity studies, and economic development reports.
- Counterpoints on environmental impact, water use, and community concerns.
- A draft briefing note with a structured evidence table linking claims to sources.

**Question 2. What is Wide Research?**
Definition: Wide research is the practice of casting a broad net to capture diverse perspectives, jurisdictions, and emerging ideas. It emphasizes breadth and comparative awareness.

What it means for AI:
- Rapidly scans across domains, sectors, and jurisdictions.
- Aggregates multiple perspectives into comparative summaries.
- Identifies trends, outliers, and early signals that may affect decisions.
- Makes broad scans feasible in hours instead of weeks.

What it means for Government:
- Provides a comprehensive view of global and national practices.
- Helps anticipate risks and opportunities before they surface locally.
- Informs cross-ministry collaboration by connecting diverse policy areas.
- Reduces blind spots and avoids duplicating efforts already tested elsewhere.

Example in Action (Data Centers):
Policy question: “How are other jurisdictions managing the energy footprint of large-scale data centers?”
Wide research with AI could produce:

- A table comparing policies: renewable energy mandates (Oregon), moratoriums (Netherlands), efficiency standards (EU).
- Notes on innovative practices such as district heating from waste energy.
- A synthesis of international lessons to inform Alberta’s policy options.

options: To generate as many sources as possible
To produce defensive, evidence-based outputs
To scan across jurisdictions and find outliers
To identify emerging risks early

sections.title: Discovering Platforms for Deep Research and Wide Research with AI

content.value:
1. **Manus** (Deep Research)

**Strengths:** Step-by-step structured workflows for research, drafting, and synthesis. Exportable outputs (documents, slide decks).

**Use Case:** Policy analysts building reproducible evidence-based memos, briefings, or synthesis reports.

**Deep or Wide:** Primarily Deep, but can also help with broad evidence collection if prompted.

**Perplexity.ai** (Wide Research)

**Strengths:** Fast horizon scanning, real-time web integration, transparent citations.

**Use Case:** Jurisdictional scans, quick cross-country comparisons, early signal detection.

**Deep or Wide:** Primarily Wide, excellent for breadth and discovery.

**GPT Deep Research (OpenAI)** (Deep Research)

**Strengths:** Extended reasoning mode for research questions, creates multi-step chains of thought, organizes findings into summaries, tables, and evidence maps.

**Use Case:** In-depth exploration of one policy problem or technical topic, with reasoning chains visible.

**Deep or Wide:** Deep.

**NotebookLM** (Deep Research, Storage & Synthesis)

**Strengths:** Upload and organize large collections of documents, query them with AI, cross-reference findings.

**Use Case:** Long-term policy files, ongoing multi-document research projects.

**Deep or Wide:** Deep.

sections.title: How to apply the T.R.U.S.T. Framework for Research?

content.value: **The T.R.U.S.T. framework** is a practical checklist to help public servants evaluate whether AI-assisted research can be trusted and safely used in decision-making. It ensures that research outputs are transparent, reproducible, and defensible.
T.R.U.S.T. stands for:

value: Traceability
Reliability
Uncertainty
Sensitivity & Safety
Triangulation

content.value: **Traceability**: every claim in your research should be traceable back to its original source. Without clear provenance, findings cannot be defended.

How AI helps:
Generates tables mapping “Claim ↔ Source.”
Links statements to government reports, academic studies, or datasets.

Example (Data Centers):
If AI states, “Data centers in Alberta consume 150 megawatts,” the output should clearly link to the Alberta Electric System Operator report, not just a vague reference.
**Reliability**: the quality of research depends on the quality of the sources. Reliable sources are authoritative, current, and relevant.

How AI helps:

Can rank or label sources by credibility (peer-reviewed, government-issued, industry white papers, etc.).

Flags lower-quality sources for manual review.

Example (Data Centers):
An International Energy Agency (IEA) report on global electricity use is more reliable than a personal blog about data center cooling.
**Uncertainty**: good research acknowledges what is not known. AI should highlight gaps, inconsistencies, or areas where evidence is weak.

How AI helps:
Can summarize areas of disagreement in the literature.
Generates “confidence notes” when data is sparse or conflicting.

Example (Data Centers):
If water use estimates for hyperscale data centers range from 1 to 5 million liters per day, AI should present the range and note uncertainty rather than fixating on a single number.
**Sensitivity & Safety**: research must account for risks — legal, cultural, environmental, or political. Outputs that ignore sensitivities can cause harm or controversy.

How AI helps:

Flags sensitive policy implications.

Can run compliance or safety checks against pre-set frameworks (e.g., FOIP, environmental standards).

Example (Data Centers):
If AI recommends new zoning fast-tracks for data centers, it should also flag risks such as community pushback, land-use conflicts, or environmental sensitivities.
**Triangulation**: strong claims are supported by multiple, independent sources. Triangulation builds confidence by cross-verifying evidence.

How AI helps:

Aggregates findings across different datasets, reports, and jurisdictions.

Highlights where multiple sources agree or disagree.

Example (Data Centers):
If Canada, the EU, and the U.S. all report rising grid strain due to hyperscale centers, that triangulated evidence is stronger than a single case study.

**Why T.R.U.S.T. Matters**

By applying T.R.U.S.T., public servants can:

Rapidly filter AI outputs into usable evidence vs. weak or unverifiable claims.

Ensure research workflows are transparent and reproducible.

sections.title: From Research to Artifacts and Applications

content.value:
1. **What do we want to do with deep research?**

Deep research is not just about finding answers — it’s about producing usable, defensible outputs that drive decisions. In government, the goal is to turn complex information into formats that:

**Support decision-making** (briefing notes, issue papers).

**Clarify trade-offs** (options tables, argument maps).

**Communicate clearly** (slide decks, infographics).

**Stand up to scrutiny** (with sources and reproducibility built in).

**AI’s role:** AI accelerates this process by taking raw research and transforming it into structured outputs that can be shared with executives, teams, and stakeholders.

**What are the artifacts government makes?**

Government research usually results in artifacts that are standardized, recognizable, and policy-relevant. Common ones include:

**Briefing notes** — concise, defensible summaries for ministers and deputies.

**Issue papers / memos** — deeper dives into a problem or proposal.

**Options tables** — side-by-side comparisons of choices with pros, cons, and costs.

**Jurisdictional scan tables** — how other regions address similar issues.

**Slide decks** — executive-ready presentations that summarize evidence and recommendations.

**Argument maps** — visuals that show claims, counterclaims, and supporting evidence.

**Environmental scans** — broad summaries of trends and external risks.

**AI’s role:** AI can generate first drafts of these artifacts directly from research outputs, making the analyst’s role one of verification, refinement, and judgment.

**How can we turn research into apps, artifacts, and briefings?**

The real opportunity with AI is scaling artifacts into interactive tools. Instead of static documents, research can become living systems:

**From briefing note → Dashboard**
A static briefing note on data centers’ energy use becomes a live dashboard that updates automatically with new grid data.

**From options table → Decision app**
A comparative table of policy options becomes an interactive app where executives can explore costs, risks, and outcomes dynamically.

**From environmental scan → Early warning system**
A wide research scan becomes a “radar” that tracks signals, alerts analysts, and highlights emerging risks.

**From knowledge graph → Policy navigation tool**
A deep research project produces a structured knowledge graph that becomes searchable through chat interfaces.

**Clever Insight:** Once research is standardized — claims, sources, arguments, tables — AI can pipeline it directly into different formats: documents, slides, dashboards, or even citizen-facing apps. This makes research reusable, scalable, and continuously valuable rather than locked in one memo.

**Takeaway for Participants**

Deep research = evidence → but its real value comes when turned into artifacts.

Artifacts = briefing notes, memos, tables, slides → standard forms government uses.

Next-level: AI allows artifacts to evolve into apps and living tools that continuously update and inform.

sections.title: What happens if AI gets things wrong?

content.value:
**Why AI Can Get Things Wrong**

AI research tools are powerful, but they are not perfect. They can:

**Hallucinate** (fabricate facts or citations).

**Over-simplify** complex data.

**Miss nuance** in sensitive contexts.

**Overstate certainty** where uncertainty exists.

This doesn’t mean the tool is useless — it means the human role is verification. Think of AI as a *research assistant who works quickly, but needs supervision*.

**Why We Can’t Read Everything**

In government, time is short and outputs can be long. We rarely have the luxury of reviewing every line of every AI-generated note or scan. Instead, the goal is to verify efficiently — focusing on the most important claims and sources.

**How to Verify AI Outputs**

**A. Use the T.R.U.S.T. Framework**
Quickly check:

**Traceability:** Are claims linked to real sources?

**Reliability:** Are those sources credible?

**Uncertainty:** Are gaps and unknowns highlighted?

**Sensitivity & Safety:** Are risks or sensitive issues flagged?

**Triangulation:** Are multiple sources aligned on the same point?

**B. Spot-Check, Don’t Over-Read**

Pick the top 3–5 claims.

Verify those sources directly.

If they hold up, confidence in the rest increases.

**C. Compare with Peers**

Ask multiple participants or teams to research the same question.

Compare their artifacts and outputs to see where results converge or diverge.

**D. Use AI to Self-Verify**

Ask the model: *“Show me the sources for this claim.”*

Or: *“List counter-arguments that might challenge this conclusion.”*

Example (Data Centers)

AI generates a note: *“Alberta data centers are responsible for 3% of provincial electricity consumption.”*

Verification steps:

**Traceability:** Is there a citation from AESO (Alberta Electric System Operator)?

**Reliability:** Government or utility source > blog post.

**Uncertainty:** Is the number consistent with other reports, or is it a rough estimate?

**Triangulation:** Do federal, industry, and academic sources report similar figures?

**Result:** If verified, the claim can stay in the briefing note. If not, mark it as uncertain.

**Key Takeaway**

AI will get things wrong — expect it.

Analysts don’t need to read everything — they need to verify the critical claims efficiently.

By using **T.R.U.S.T., spot-checking, and peer comparison**, public servants can turn fast AI scans into defensible government outputs.

sections.title: Concept: Risks and Ethical Considerations using AI in research

content.value: Using AI in research introduces several risks that you must actively manage.

**1. Hallucination and Fabrication**

AI models can generate **plausible-sounding but entirely false information**. This is especially dangerous in research, where a fabricated citation or statistic can undermine your credibility.

**Mitigation strategies:**

value: Always verify claims against original sources.
Use AI tools that provide citations and check those citations.
Be especially skeptical of specific numbers, dates, and quotes.

content.value:
**2. Over-Reliance and Deskilling**

If you always delegate research to AI, you may lose the ability to critically evaluate sources, identify gaps, or develop deep domain expertise.

**Mitigation strategies:**

value: Use AI for breadth, but do some deep reading yourself.
Treat AI outputs as a starting point, not a final answer.
Maintain your own research skills through regular practice.

content.value:
**Best Practices for AI-Assisted Research**

Here's how we recommend you work with AI tools:

value: **Start with a clear question**: The more specific your research question, the better AI output will be.
**Verify critical claims:** Check citations, cross-reference facts, and consult original sources for key findings.
**Diversify your sources:** Don't rely solely on AI-gathered sources. Add your own domain expertise and known authoritative sources.
**Document your process:** Keep track of what AI tools you used, what prompts you gave, and how you verified outputs.
**Maintain human oversight:** You are the final arbiter of quality, relevance, and ethical use.

content.value:
**Key Concepts**

What is **Deep Research**?

**Deep research** is the intensive, focused analysis of a small number of high-quality sources to understand nuance, verify claims, and generate original insights. It prioritizes **depth over breadth**. If wide research is the satellite map, deep research is the geological survey of a specific, promising location.

**Core Goals of Deep Research:**

value: **Verification:** To fact-check claims, check citations, and confirm data points against original sources.
**Critical Analysis:** To evaluate the methodology, assumptions, and potential biases of a source.
**Nuance Extraction:** To understand complex arguments, counterarguments, and the fine details of a topic.
**Insight Generation:** To synthesize information from multiple high-quality sources to form a new, evidence-based conclusion.

content.value: **When to Use Deep Research:**

value: **After Wide Research:** To investigate the most promising or important sources identified during your initial scan.
**Critical Fact-Checking:** When a specific claim, statistic, or quote is central to your argument and must be verified.
**Expert-Level Understanding:** When you need to become a subject matter expert on a narrow topic.
**Analyzing Primary Sources:** When working with complex documents like legal texts, scientific papers, or lengthy government reports.

content.value: To bring all these concepts together, let’s look at a real-world workflow used in modern application development from Deputy Minister Janak Alford's Masterclass, called "Hydrating Requirements to Apps." This process shows how different AI tools work together to take a raw idea and turn it into a fully realized, enterprise-ready application. This is a perfect example of combining wide and deep research with iterative development.

**Step 1: Capturing Business Requirements with Transcription Tool**

**The workflow begins in the real world of business meetings**. Your team discusses an opportunity, a need, or a problem during a Microsoft Teams meeting (or in-person, or other platform). Rather than relying on handwritten notes or memory, you use  transcription tool to automatically capture the entire conversation. This transcript becomes your **raw, unfiltered source of business requirements**.

This step is crucial because it preserves the original context and nuance that often gets lost when requirements are translated through multiple people. The transcript might be **messy, conversational, and full of tangents, but it contains the seeds of what needs to be built**.

**Step 2: Expanding Key Concepts with Regular AI**

Next, you take the Teams transcript and feed it to a regular conversational AI like Albert, ChatGPT, or Microsoft Copilot. Your prompt might be: *"Read this meeting transcript and identify the key concepts, features, and requirements mentioned. Expand on each one with more detail and suggest related considerations."*

The AI acts as an intelligent assistant that:

• Extracts the core ideas from the conversational noise

• Expands each concept with additional context, potential features, and related considerations

• Organizes the information into a more structured format

• Suggests angles or features that weren't explicitly mentioned but are implied

This is a **creative expansion** step. The AI is helping you move from **raw conversation** to a **more structured understanding of what's being asked for**. However, at this stage, nothing has been validated against reality. It's still just ideas and possibilities.

**Step 3: Hydrating with AI Research**

This is where **AI research** comes in, and this is the critical "hydration" step. You take the expanded concepts from Step 2 and ask AI to hydrate them with research. What does "hydrating" mean in this context?

Hydrating means **adding substance, evidence, and reality to ideas**. AI transforms abstract concepts into grounded, evidence-based insights by:

• **Validating the Core Idea:** Does this problem actually exist? Is there market evidence? What do experts say?

• **Finding Real-World Examples:** I search for case studies, existing implementations, and comparable products or policies.

• **Identifying Pros and Cons:** I conduct deep research to uncover the advantages and risks based on actual data, not speculation.

• **Providing Context:** I find relevant statistics, market trends, regulatory considerations, and technical constraints.

• **Cross-Referencing Claims:** If the expanded concepts made assumptions, I verify them against authoritative sources.

This is where **wide** and **deep research** come together. I might do **wide research** to *scan the competitive landscape* (*"Find 20 similar products and compare their features"*) and **deep research** to *validate specific technical claims* ("*Verify whether this technology actually achieves the performance mentioned*").

The output of this step is a research-backed, evidence-rich document that grounds the original ideas in reality. You now know **not just what people want to build, but whether it's viable, what the risks are, and what the market looks like**.

**Step 4: The Refine, Challenge, and Expand Loop**

The findings from deep research feed into a critical iterative loop that leads to the first prototype. This loop involves:

• **Refine:** The initial concept is improved and sharpened based on the evidence I provided.

• **Challenge:** The team and I critically question the refined concept. Where are its weak points? What assumptions are we making?

• **Expand:** This is a wide, comparative research step. Here, I would be tasked to compare the refined concept against existing products, different regulatory environments, or alternative approaches. For example, I might be asked to create a comparison table of 10 competitor products.

This loop, which typically iterates around 5 times, ensures **the concept is robust, well-understood, and validated** before any significant development resources are committed. The output is a **throwaway first prototype** designed solely to confirm a **shared understanding of the requirements**.

**Step 5: Formal Specification and Development**

Once the prototype validates the core requirements, the project moves into a more traditional software development lifecycle:

• A formal Business and Technical Specification is created.

• Sprinting begins, with developers building the application based on enterprise standards.

• The process involves extensive testing and iteration (50-100 cycles), user acceptance testing (UAT), and final sign-off before deployment.

sections.title: Apply AI to Your Base Role

content.value:
**Objective 1:**

Conduct an AI-assisted deep research project on a policy, program, or operational question directly relevant to your role in government. Your task is to investigate the opportunities, challenges, and implications of that issue, and produce artifacts that are usable in your ministry or branch.

Focus on questions such as:

What is one decision, problem, or briefing topic you regularly face?

What evidence do you need to support leadership or colleagues on that issue?

How have other jurisdictions managed this issue, and what lessons are transferable?

What options or recommendations could you propose based on credible evidence?

Deliverables

Executive Brief (≤2 pages): Situation, key findings with citations, and implications for your ministry/branch.

Claim ↔ Source Evidence Table: Each claim linked to a credible source.

Jurisdictional Scan Table: Comparison of at least three other regions, agencies, or organizations relevant to your issue.

Options Memo (short): Two or three potential approaches for your ministry/branch, with pros, cons, and risks.

Slide Deck (5–7 slides): Condensed summary, prepared for your manager, director, or ADM.

Success Criteria

Outputs are transparent, evidence-based, and reproducible.

You apply the T.R.U.S.T. framework to verify accuracy.

Research addresses a real problem or decision in your day-to-day work.

Deliverables are clear, actionable, and immediately usable by your team.

**Objective 2:**

Conduct an AI-assisted wide research (horizon scan) to map the trends, signals, and emerging issues most relevant to your ministry or program area. Your task is to identify weak signals and converging trends that could affect your role in the near term (0–12 months), mid term (1–3 years), and long term (3–10 years), and translate them into policy-ready insights for your home team.

Focus on questions such as:

What trends or signals could disrupt your ministry’s work in the next few years?

What are other jurisdictions, agencies, or sectors doing that Alberta should watch?

What early warnings should your leadership team monitor now?

How could your branch prepare for risks or opportunities on the horizon?

Deliverables

Executive Horizon Scan (≤2 pages): Situation snapshot with citations, top 3–5 trend clusters (with confidence and time horizon), and implications for your ministry/branch.

Signal Register (CSV/Markdown): 20–40 diverse, recent signals tagged with domain, geography, confidence, novelty, and policy relevance.

Trend Cards (2–3): Clear summaries of top trends with citations, drivers, uncertainties, and policy implications.

Jurisdictional Scan Table: At least two other jurisdictions’ approaches to a comparable issue.

Slide Deck (5–7 slides): Condensed briefing for your team or executive.

Success Criteria

Outputs are transparent, traceable, and defensible.

You apply the T.R.U.S.T. framework (Traceability, Reliability, Uncertainty, Sensitivity & Safety, Triangulation).

Research reflects signals and trends directly relevant to your base role.

Deliverables are clear, accessible, and ready to brief to leadership.

👉 **End Goal**: You leave the AI Academy not only having practiced deep and wide research, but also with real, role-specific artifacts (briefs, tables, decks) that you can take back to your branch, show your leadership, and apply immediately.

*Wide Research Challenge: Data Centers and Government Policy*

**Objective**

Conduct an AI-assisted wide research (horizon scan) to map how the growth of large-scale data centers may affect Alberta over the near term (0–12 months), mid term (1–3 years), and long term (3–10 years). Your task is to surface emerging issues, weak signals, converging trends, and policy implications across jurisdictions, and present a policy-ready synthesis that informs strategy, risk posture, and next steps.

Focus on questions such as:

What trends are driving global data center growth (AI/compute demand, edge vs. hyperscale, renewable PPAs, cooling innovations)?

Where are early signals of risk or opportunity for Alberta (grid constraints, interconnection queues, water or land-use pressures, waste-heat reuse, permitting timelines)?

How are comparator jurisdictions (e.g., BC/ON/QC, Virginia/Oregon/Texas, Ireland/Netherlands/Denmark, Singapore/Japan/Korea) balancing competitiveness with sustainability and community trust?

Which indicators should Alberta monitor to anticipate issues early (e.g., queue MW, renewable share, PUE/WUE ranges, permit backlogs, moratoriums)?

**Deliverables**

Participants will produce:

*Executive Horizon Scan (≤2 pages):* Situation snapshot with citations, top signals and trend clusters (with confidence and time horizon), implications for Alberta, and early actions.

*Signal Register (CSV/Markdown):* 30–60 recent, diverse signals tagged with domain, geography, source tier, confidence, novelty, momentum, policy relevance, time horizon, and locator/quote.

*Trend Cards (Top 4–6):* Title, definition, drivers, representative signals with citations, key statistics, uncertainties, intersections, policy implications, and indicators to watch.

*Jurisdictional Scan Table:* Side-by-side comparison of at least three regions’ policy approaches (incentives, siting/permits, energy/water/efficiency standards, heat-recovery programs).

*Slide Deck (5–7 slides):* Condensed briefing of the scan, trend cards, and recommended early actions (Gamma or another AI tool).

**Success Criteria**

Outputs are transparent, evidence-based, and reproducible.

Participants apply the T.R.U.S.T. framework to tag traceability, reliability, uncertainty, sensitivity/safety, and triangulation.

Research reflects a balanced view across economic, environmental, infrastructure, and community perspectives.

content.value: Understanding the fundamentals of AI agents, their components, and capabilities

AI agents are autonomous (or semi-autonomous) software systems that can perceive information, reason about it, make decisions, and take actions toward a defined goal. Think of them as "digital workers" that combine large language models (like GPT) with tools, memory, and policies to operate in real environments.

**Key Properties**

Autonomy – they can initiate actions without waiting for a user’s every instruction.

Goal-driven – they’re designed around objectives (e.g., “summarize research papers,” “book a meeting,” “manage cloud deployments”).

Reasoning – they can plan multi-step tasks, break problems down, and adjust strategies dynamically.

Perception – they take in context: user input, data streams, APIs, or even sensor feeds.

Action – they execute via connected tools: APIs, databases, emails, code execution, or other software systems.

Memory – advanced agents keep track of past interactions or accumulated knowledge to refine decisions.

**Types of AI Agents**

Reactive agents – respond to inputs immediately, no memory (e.g., chatbots that only answer queries).

Deliberative agents – plan before acting, often simulate outcomes (e.g., scheduling assistants).

Learning agents – adapt over time, improve through reinforcement or feedback (e.g., trading bots).

Multi-agent systems – networks of agents collaborating or competing to solve complex problems (e.g., swarm intelligence, multi-bot workflows).

**Real-World Examples**

Customer service agents (answering, triaging, escalating issues)

Personal productivity bots (scheduling, summarizing, drafting content)

DevOps assistants (deploying infrastructure, running tests, monitoring systems)

Research copilots (scanning literature, extracting insights, generating reports)

Game or simulation agents (NPCs that act intelligently in dynamic worlds)
Tracing the evolution from language models to autonomous agents
How did large language models evolve into agentic AI systems?

**Tracing the Evolution from Language Models to Autonomous Agents**

**Language Models (LLMs) as Predictors**

Early LLMs like GPT-2 were powerful text predictors: they generated human-like responses but had no memory, goals, or ability to interact with the outside world.

Their scope was narrow: respond to prompts, generate text, and stay confined within the chat interface.

**LLMs with Tools (Augmented Models)**

The next step was connecting models to calculators, databases, APIs, and search engines.

Instead of “hallucinating” facts, they could call a tool, fetch real data, and return accurate results.

This bridged the gap between pure text prediction and problem-solving.

**LLMs with Memory and Context**

Agents started to gain working memory (short-term context) and long-term memory (persisted knowledge).

This allowed them to learn from prior interactions, track user goals, and adapt over time.

**LLMs as Planners**

Prompt engineering evolved into multi-step reasoning frameworks (e.g., chain-of-thought, tree-of-thought, ReAct).

Instead of producing a single answer, models could plan: break down a problem, reason through alternatives, and execute sequential steps.

**Agentic AI (Autonomous Systems)**

Today’s frontier: AI agents that perceive, reason, act, and adapt.

They can:

Set and pursue goals with minimal human prompting

Use tools, APIs, and other software systems

Collaborate with other agents in multi-agent environments

Improve via reinforcement or feedback loops

Instead of “smart autocomplete,” they function more like digital colleagues—handling workflows, managing projects, or simulating organizations.

**The Road Ahead**

Agentic AI is pushing toward systems that are not just assistants but autonomous operators.

Challenges remain: reliability, safety, alignment, and governance.

But the direction is clear: we’re moving from language models that generate text to intelligent agents that get things done.
Exploring agent frameworks, workflows, and practical implementations

**Exploring Agent Frameworks, Workflows, and Practical Implementations**

**From Single Tasks to Workflows**

Basic LLM usage: one-off Q&A or text generation.

Agent usage: multi-step workflows where reasoning, tool use, and memory combine.

Example: “research a market, generate a summary, draft outreach emails, and schedule meetings.”

**Core Agent Workflow Components**

Perception/Input – capture goals, prompts, or external data.

Planning – break objectives into steps (Chain-of-Thought, ReAct, Tree-of-Thought).

Action Execution – call APIs, trigger code, update databases, or communicate.

Feedback Loop – monitor outcomes, verify success, retry if needed.

Memory – short-term (context of current session) and long-term (history, knowledge base).

**Agent Frameworks**

LangChain – orchestration layer for LLMs + tools + memory.

AutoGPT / BabyAGI – early autonomous agent demos that highlighted both potential and limitations.

CrewAI, MetaGPT, OpenAgents – frameworks for multi-agent collaboration, specializing roles and responsibilities.

Custom Implementations – enterprises increasingly building proprietary frameworks tuned to security, compliance, and integration needs.

**Workflow Patterns in Practice**

Linear automation – sequential tasks (e.g., document processing → extract data → file storage).

Decision branching – agents evaluate options, then choose a path (e.g., support triage).

Human-in-the-loop – agents propose, humans approve, agents execute.

Multi-agent collaboration – specialized agents (researcher, planner, executor) coordinate.

**Practical Implementations**

Business: AI assistants that handle customer support tickets end-to-end.

Government: policy search agents that parse regulations and generate compliance reports.

Engineering: DevOps agents that detect issues, open tickets, and patch systems automatically.

Creative: multi-agent studios where “writer,” “editor,” and “designer” agents produce content together.

**Challenges and Opportunities**

Reliability (avoiding errors in long chains of tasks).

Security (safe tool usage, data governance).

Evaluation (measuring agent performance).

Opportunity: agent workflows reduce manual overhead and unlock scalable, autonomous operations across industries.
