content.value: Welcome to the n8n nodes module! In n8n, a node represents a single step or action in your workflow. Think of them as building blocks that you connect together to automate tasks. Each node performs a specific function, such as fetching data from an API, transforming data, or sending an email.
Nodes have inputs and outputs. The output of one node can be connected to the input of another, creating a chain of actions. This allows you to build complex workflows by combining simple nodes.
n8n offers a wide variety of nodes, categorized by their function. Some common categories include:

value: **Trigger Nodes:** Start your workflow based on an event (e.g., a new email, a webhook call).
**Action Nodes:** Perform actions like sending emails, creating files, or updating databases.
**Transformation Nodes:** Modify data, such as filtering, mapping, or converting formats.
**Integration Nodes:** Connect to third-party services like Google Sheets, Twitter, or Slack.

content.value: Understanding the different types of nodes is crucial for designing effective workflows.
Each node has its own configuration options that determine how it behaves. These options can include API keys, file paths, data mappings, and other settings specific to the node's function.

value: **Credentials:** Securely store API keys and other sensitive information.
**Parameters:** Define the specific actions the node should perform (e.g., the subject and body of an email).
**Input Data:** Specify how the node should receive data from previous nodes.

content.value: Properly configuring your nodes is essential for ensuring your workflows function correctly.

sections.title: Practical Example: Sending a Slack Message

content.value: Let's walk through a simple example of using nodes to send a Slack message. This workflow will consist of two nodes:

value: **Manual Trigger Node:** This node will manually trigger the workflow.
**Slack Node:** This node will send a message to a specified Slack channel.

content.value: First, add a Manual Trigger node to your workflow. Then, add a Slack node and configure it with your Slack API credentials and the channel you want to send the message to. Connect the output of the Manual Trigger node to the input of the Slack node. Finally, add the text you would like to send as a parameter to the Slack node.
Now, when you execute the workflow, it will send a message to your Slack channel.

sections.title: Why Voice Matters in AI Interactions

content.value:
Hydration is the process of transforming raw, spoken (or written) information, and having the AI expand it and add structure.

It can begin with a recorded conversation—such as an interview, planning discussion, or brainstorming session. The AI generates a transcript and then expands on it - based on your direction. The system identifies key ideas, fills gaps, reorganizes concepts, and formats the content into usable outputs such as summaries, briefing notes, requirements documents, or full business cases.

 

Hydration through voice captures “thinking in motion,” and expands it, preserving natural communication while producing structured, high-quality outputs. This reduces administrative workload and speeds up the creation of official materials.

Future AI systems will be able to understand context across multiple channels at once — speech, tone, visuals, documents, and the surrounding environment. This creates a more complete understanding of user intent.

As these capabilities expand, AI will function more like a collaborator than a tool. It will be able to listen, watch, read, summarize, and support ongoing work. AI will monitor tasks in the background, provide reminders, and continue working even after the user stops interacting.

 

This evolution supports agentic workflows, where AI not only assists but independently progresses work. The future of multimodal AI is continuous partnership, enabling technology to support tasks from start to finish.

json_data.title: 2.6.2 n8n Beginner Course - How does n8n handle data?

sections.title: Introduction to Data Handling in n8n

content.value: n8n workflows are built around the concept of data flowing between nodes. Each node receives data, processes it, and then passes it on to the next node in the workflow. Understanding how n8n represents and manipulates this data is crucial for building effective workflows.

In n8n, data is primarily represented as JSON objects. These objects can contain various data types, including strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, and even nested objects. Each node operates on these JSON objects, modifying them or extracting information as needed.
n8n utilizes JSON-like structures to manage data. This allows for a flexible and organized way to represent information. Understanding these structures is key to effectively using n8n.

value: **JSON Objects:** The fundamental building block, containing key-value pairs.
**Arrays:** Ordered lists of values, useful for handling multiple items.
**Strings:** Textual data.
**Numbers:** Numerical data (integers and decimals).
**Booleans:** True or False values.

content.value: Nodes can manipulate these structures using expressions, functions, and other built-in tools. For example, you can use the `{{ $json.propertyName }}` syntax to access a specific property within a JSON object.

A key concept in n8n is the 'item list'. Many nodes operate on lists of items, processing each item individually. This allows you to handle multiple pieces of data efficiently within a single workflow.

For example, if you have a list of customer records, you can use a 'Split Out Items' node to process each customer individually. Then, you can use a 'Set' node to modify specific properties of each customer record.

value: **Split Out Items:** Splits a list of items into individual items.
**Merge:** Combines multiple items into a single item or list.
**Function:** Allows you to write custom JavaScript code to manipulate data.
**Set:** Modifies the properties of an item.

data.name: 1.6.1 Wide Research in the Public Sector

json_data.title: 1.6.1 Wide Research in the Public Sector

content.value:
Wide research is a **breadth-first approach to research**. Its purpose is to understand the full landscape surrounding an issue before narrowing toward specific options or decisions.

Wide research focuses on:

value: Identifying relevant actors, approaches, and jurisdictions
Surfacing patterns, themes, and emerging trends
Highlighting uncertainties and knowledge gaps
Preventing blind spots early in the process

content.value: Wide research does not aim to reach final conclusions. Instead, it establishes context and ensures that subsequent analysis is grounded in a comprehensive understanding of what exists.
Wide research is not:

value: A final recommendation
A detailed evaluation of a single option
A replacement for judgment or decision-making
Proof that an approach is "best"

content.value: Its value lies in **orientation**, not resolution.

sections.title: Wide Research in the Public Sector Context

content.value: In the public sector, wide research plays a critical role at the **front end of policy, program, and operational work**.
It is commonly used to:

value: Scan how other jurisdictions are approaching similar issues
Identify policy models, delivery mechanisms, or regulatory approaches
Understand stakeholder perspectives and interests
Anticipate risks, sensitivities, and unintended consequences
Support early briefings and issue identification

content.value: Because public-sector decisions must be transparent and defensible, wide research helps demonstrate that options were explored thoughtfully and that decisions were not made in isolation.

sections.title: Why Wide Research Matters in Government

content.value: Wide research helps ensure that:

value: The problem is framed correctly
Obvious options are not missed
Novelty is not mistaken for effectiveness
Early assumptions are tested against reality

content.value: By expanding awareness before narrowing focus, wide research reduces the risk of prematurely committing to incomplete or biased solutions.
Wide research often produces:

value: Landscape overviews
Jurisdictional scans
Option inventories
High-level comparison summaries
Lists of open questions and uncertainties

content.value: These outputs are designed to inform next steps, not close the file.

Wide research is usually followed by **deep research**.

Once the landscape is understood, deep research focuses effort on a smaller number of high-impact areas, enabling rigorous analysis, evidence testing, and decision-grade recommendations.

AI-enabled research strengthens wide research by accelerating scanning, organizing large volumes of information, and making patterns visible while still requiring human judgment to interpret relevance and implications.

**Key Takeaway**

Wide research helps ensure we are looking in the right places before deciding what to do.

content.value: Welcome to the AI Prompting Masterclass! In this module, we'll explore the essentials of crafting effective prompts for AI models. Prompting is the art and science of guiding AI to produce the desired results. Understanding prompting techniques is crucial for leveraging the full potential of AI.

Think of a prompt as a question or instruction you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly impacts the quality of the AI's response. A well-crafted prompt can unlock creativity, solve problems, and automate tasks.
Several key concepts are fundamental to effective prompting:

value: **Clarity:** Your prompt should be clear and unambiguous. Avoid jargon or vague language.
**Specificity:** Be specific about what you want the AI to do. The more details you provide, the better the results.
**Context:** Provide the AI with relevant context to understand the task at hand.
**Constraints:** Define any limitations or boundaries for the AI's response.
**Iteration:** Prompting is often an iterative process. Experiment with different prompts and refine them based on the AI's output.

content.value: Here are some common prompting techniques:

value: **Zero-Shot Prompting:** Asking the AI to perform a task without providing any examples.
**Few-Shot Prompting:** Providing the AI with a few examples to guide its response.
**Chain-of-Thought Prompting:** Encouraging the AI to explain its reasoning process step-by-step.
**Role-Playing:** Asking the AI to assume a specific role or persona.

content.value: Let's look at an example of zero-shot prompting: 'Translate "Hello, world!" to Spanish.'

Now, an example of few-shot prompting: 'Translate the following English phrases to French:
English: Hello, world!
French: Bonjour le monde!
English: How are you?
French: Comment allez-vous?
English: Good morning!
French:'

value: **Start Simple:** Begin with a basic prompt and gradually add complexity.

sections.title: Introduction to Copilot Agents in SPO

content.value:
**What is a Copilot agent in SharePoint Online (SPO)?**  
A Copilot agent in SPO is like a built-in AI helper that works directly with the data in your SharePoint site. It can answer questions, find information, and guide you through tasks by using the documents, pages, and files already stored in that site. Because the agent is tied to your site’s content, its answers are more accurate and relevant.

**Example use case**  
Imagine your legal team has a SharePoint library containing legal opinions, statutes, and case law. Instead of searching through hundreds of files, the agent can quickly pull out the right insights, helping the team avoid duplicate work and stay consistent by reusing past knowledge.

**Why use it?**  

•   Helps you work faster by reducing repetitive tasks  
•   Keeps answers consistent across your team  
•   Lets you share agents with colleagues who also have a Copilot license, so the whole group benefits from the same streamlined experience

**Important note**  

•  If you can’t see all the agent’s sources, its answers may be incomplete  
•   A SharePoint admin may need to update permissions if broader access is required

content.value:
**Worked Example – Copilot Agent for Policy Enquiries**  
Scenario: General staff across the organization often email or call the policy team with questions like “What is our stance on generative AI tools?” or “Has government published guidelines on AI ethics?” Analysts spend hours digging through SharePoint to locate relevant guidelines, standards and policies to provide responses. A SPO Copilot agent could streamline this.  

   

**1) What’s the Problem?**  
“Staff ask frequent questions about AI policies and guidelines. Analysts spend significant time finding the right documents. We need an agent that retrieves relevant AI policy documents and provides short, plain-language answers.”  

   

**2) Why Use an Agent?**  
• Questions are repetitive and come from many staff.  
• The answers exist but are spread across multiple libraries.  
• An agent can save analyst time and ensure consistent messaging.  

   

**3) What Data Matters?**  
• SharePoint site: e.g. Digital Policy Repository  
• Libraries: AI Guidelines, Standards and Policies  
• File types: DOCX and PDF  

   

**4) What’s the Agent’s Role?**  
• Retriever → locate AI-related documents.  
• Summarizer → produce 3–5 bullet overviews of key points.  
• Drafting Assistant → generate short, plain-language responses staff can reuse.  

   

**5) What Instructions Will Guide It?**  
• Prompts (user side): “What guidance do we have on staff using AI for drafting documents?”  

• System Instructions (RICECO):  
  **Role:** You are a public-sector policy analyst. Your job is to respond to staff enquiries by retrieving and summarizing AI-related guidelines, standards, and policy documents that you have access to, providing clear, plain-language answers that link back to the original sources.  
  **Input:** User’s question or keywords about AI.  
  **Context:** Search only the files that you have access to.  
  **Execution:** Find the most relevant files, extract key information, and present it clearly.  
  **Constraints:**  
      • Plain-language answers under 150 words.  
      • Always include file names with links.  
      • Do not invent new policies or positions.  
  **Output:**  
      • A bullet-point summary linked to source documents.  
      • Optionally, a draft email reply staff could send.  

   

**6) What Outputs Do You Need?**  
• Linked summary: Document Title | Date | Link | 3–5 Key Points.  
• Short response draft: Plain-language text staff can copy into an email or Teams reply.

Create an agent in SPO and share your findings in the chat. Include:  
 

• **The problem it solves** → What pain point or challenge led you to create this agent?  
• **The purpose** → What the agent is designed to do and why it’s useful.  
• **The data it uses** → What is the format and type of data.  
• **The outputs it provides** → What form the results take (summary, table, bullets, etc.).

data.description: This module is designed to refresh your prompting skills from level 1 training. Those skills will be the foundation to your learning in level 2. You’ll revisit why effective prompting matters, learn to verify outputs by separating normal errors, simulated “AI lies” (risk behaviour), and hallucinations, and apply the T.R.U.S.T. protocol to make drafts that you can publish confidently. You’ll also refine prompts with RICECO (Role, Instruction, Context, Examples, Constraints, Output) and then bring it all together to build agents; treating RICECO as the agent’s task contract and TRUST as its verification policy, so your Agents are well structured, auditable, and aligned to public-sector standards.

json_data.title: 2.1.0 Welcome and Prompting Refresher

content.value: **Welcome back!** This module serves as a quick refresher on key concepts we've covered previously. It's designed to help you solidify your understanding and prepare you for upcoming, more advanced topics. We'll briefly review fundamental principles and then test your knowledge with interactive quizzes.

This section explains why good prompting is the fastest path to useful drafts in public-sector work. You’ll refresh how clear requests reduce ambiguity, keep the model inside your scope (Alberta audience, policy constraints, privacy), and cut down on rework. You’ll see how specifying role, purpose, audience, and output format up front leads to first drafts you can actually use that are short, structured, and easy to verify. **Set direction with a tidy prompt, and you’ll spend your time improving, not salvaging.**

**Strong and effective prompting** is the fastest path to useful, trustworthy drafts, especially in public-sector work where scope, audience, and risk matter. We’re setting the tone for Level 2: your prompts become “task contracts” for agents.

Think of the LLM as a very fast junior analyst. If you give fuzzy direction, you’ll get fuzzy work. If you give a crisp role, goal, audience, and format, you’ll get something you can use right away, then your time goes into judgement and polish, not rescue missions. In Level 2, these same skills turn into agent instructions. We’ll practice both today.”

### **Learner activity: ‘Bad → Better’ prompt fix** (2 minutes):

Pick one weak prompt and tighten it in 2 lines using role + outcome + audience + constraints.

**Weak:** “Summarize Alberta’s cloud policy.”

**Better:** “You are a GoA policy analyst. Write a 120-word brief for non-technical executives that explains Alberta’s cloud policy in plain language. Cite the exact section for any obligations and link to the latest official source.”

### **Watch-outs & tips:**

-- Avoid “just do X” prompts. Add audience and format.

-- Don’t overload with jargon; use plain language.

-- If the topic touches policy or people data, say so in the prompt (that’s part of scoping risk).

sections.title: Verify the output: errors vs. “AI lies” vs. hallucinations

content.value: When AI gets something wrong, it isn’t always the same kind of wrong and each type needs a different fix. In this refresher, you’ll quickly re-ground in the three failure modes from Level 1: **ordinary errors** (bad facts or math when a correct answer exists), confident but false **AI “lies”** (plausible-sounding claims that don’t hold up to a stronger source), and outright **hallucinations** (made-up sections, citations, or facts with no real source). By the end, you’ll be able to spot which is which in seconds and choose the right response so you are able to correct it, re-prompt and replace, or remove it entirely.

### **1) Error (ordinary mistake)**

**What it is:** A factual or reasoning mistake when a real answer exists.

**How it shows up:** wrong date, bad math, outdated policy, misread chart.

**Why it happens:** training gaps, outdated info, arithmetic/logic slip.

**Fix:** correct it with an authoritative source (don’t discard the whole draft if the rest is useful).

Example (Error):
“Service downtime is scheduled for October 2023.”
Reality: It’s October 2025. The model reused an old date.

### **2) AI “Lie”** (confident falsehood, no intent)

**What it is:** A statement that sounds authoritative but is false; the model isn’t choosing to deceive—it’s pattern-matching and over-generalizing.

**How it shows up:** authoritative tone (“As required by…”) about a thing that’s simply not true.

**Why it happens:** the prompt nudged certainty (“confirm…”, “justify…”) or the model filled gaps with the most “plausible” pattern.

**Fix:** change the prompt to allow uncertainty; ask for assumptions and confidence; demand sources. Replace the claim with sourced truth or remove it.

**Example (AI Lie):**
Per **Section 12** of Calgary’s Cloud Bylaw, **all AI must use Vendor X.”**
Reality: That blanket mandate doesn’t exist; the model stated a sweeping rule as if true.

**3) Hallucination** (fabrication with no real source)

**What it is:** The model invents a thing that doesn’t exist; such as a policy section, citation, court case, report, URL, or even a person.

**How it shows up:** non-existent section numbers, made-up citations/links, quotes that cannot be found anywhere.

**Why it happens:** the model completes patterns (e.g., legal-sounding text) even when the real item isn’t in its knowledge.

**Fix:** remove the claim; replace it only after you find a verifiable primary source.

**Example (Hallucination):**
“See **‘GOA AI Policy 2022, s. 9(3)(b)’**" (no such document/section exists).

content.value: Turn a decent draft into a publish ready one using a five-step, low-overhead pass. You’ll refresh how to attach Traceability (exact quote + link/ID for each claim), grade Reliability (type, publisher, date → keep/replace), state Uncertainty (assumptions and 0–100 confidence), scan Sensitivity & Safety (privacy, compliance, fairness, harm), and run Triangulation for high-impact statements. You’ll leave with a tiny table-style log that travels with your draft, making approvals faster and accountability clear.

value: **The TRUST steps in plain language:**
**T — Traceability:** Every claim can be traced to a specific quote and official source link/ID.
**R — Reliability:** For each source, label type/publisher/date and decide Keep or Replace.
**U — Uncertainty:** List assumptions/unknowns; include a confidence score (0–100) and a one-line why.
**S — Sensitivity & Safety:** Flag privacy, compliance, fairness, or harm risks; propose safer wording or redactions.
**T — Triangulation:** For critical claims, cross-check against 1–2 independent sources; decide Use / Revise / Reject.

content.value: **T.R.U.S.T.** is your one-minute publish check. When the output might leave your desk or influence someone else’s decision run **T.R.U.S.T.**. At minimum, always do **T** and **R**. If the stakes are higher, add **U**, **S**, and the final **T**. Keep these micro-prompts below handy and watch the value and quality of your outputs increase.

value: **T.R.U.S.T. micro-prompts (copy/paste into the model):**
**Traceability** “For each claim, paste the verbatim quote and the official URL/ID.”
**Reliability** “For each citation, label source type, publisher, and date; recommend Keep or Replace.”
**Uncertainty** “List assumptions/unknowns. Give 0–100 confidence with a 1-sentence rationale.”
**Sensitivity & Safety** “Flag privacy/compliance/fairness risks. Suggest safer wording or redactions.”
**Triangulation** “For critical claims, cross-check with 1–2 independent sources; advise Use/Revise/Reject.”
**Watch-outs & tips:**
-- If you can’t trace it, don’t publish it.
-- Reliability isn’t just “has a link”—check the date and the publisher’s authority.
-- If it touches people, money, or law, add U and S steps automatically.

content.value: RICECO shows how to ask in a way that gets back exactly what you need. You’ll refresh the six parts of RICECO—Role, Instruction, Context, Examples, Constraints, Output—and see how each one closes a common gap (e.g., audience specificity, word limits, allowed sources). You’ll practice writing a prompt you can reuse this week, with an emphasis on measurable output (e.g., “1 paragraph + 3-row table”) and source constraints (“official AB sources only”). The aim is fewer clarifying turns and a draft that’s easy to run through T.R.U.S.T.

value: **RICECO in plain language:**
**R — Role:** Who the model is (and who it’s serving).
**I — Instruction:** The task and the outcome you want.
**C — Context:** Audience, jurisdiction, policy scope, reading level, etc.
**E — Examples:** A tiny sample to set tone/structure when precision matters.
**C — Constraints:** Allowed sources, privacy rules, length limits, words to avoid.
**O — Output:** Exact sections, tables, bullet counts, or file structure.
**Copy-ready RICECO skeleton prompts (paste into the model):**
**R:** You are a [role] serving [audience].
**I:** Do [task] to achieve [purpose].
**C:** Context: [jurisdiction/policy/privacy scope/plain language].
**E:** Example snippet: “[1–2 lines showing tone/structure].”
**C:** Constraints: [allowed sources/tone/length/words to avoid].
**O:** Output as [format: e.g., 120-char SMS + 80-word web blurb + bullet list of 3 actions].
**Watch-outs & tips:**
-- Don’t skip **Output**, that’s the #1 cause of cleanup later.
-- Keep **Examples** short; they guide, they don’t replace the task.
-- For compliance-sensitive topics, put the constraints in bold terms (e.g., “No personal data. Use only [specific law/policy] as sources.”).

content.value:
### **Bringing it all together to build agents:**
With **Level 2**’s focus on **agents and agentic workflows**, you’ll see how **RICECO** becomes the “task contract” an agent follows (role, goals, guardrails, output), and how **T.R.U.S.T.** becomes the agent’s built-in verification policy (traceability checks, uncertainty notes, and triangulation triggers). You’ll learn what to encode as prompts vs. what to enforce as rules (e.g., “no speculation,” source whitelists, privacy filters), so your agents **produce auditable outputs** that meet public-sector standards. The takeaway: **clear prompts plus lightweight verification are the foundation for reliable, automatable agent behaviors.**

value: **What we covered today (and why it matters):**
-- You sharpened prompting fundamentals so your first drafts are clear, scoped, and useful—no more rescuing vague outputs.
-- You refreshed the differences between errors, AI “lies,” and hallucinations, so you can pick the right fix fast.
-- You practiced the T.R.U.S.T. protocol as a one-minute publish check for traceability, reliability, uncertainty, safety, and triangulation.
-- You used RICECO to turn fuzzy asks into crisp “task contracts” that models (and soon, agents) can execute consistently.
**How these fit together for Level 2 (agents & agentic workflows):**
**RICECO = the agent’s job description.** Role, Instruction, Context, Examples, Constraints, Output format; this becomes the blueprint your agent follows every time.
**T.R.U.S.T. = the agent’s verification policy.** Build checks into the workflow (trace quotes, label sources/dates, escalate uncertainty, auto-triangulate high-impact claims).
**Error/Lie/Hallucination literacy = risk controls.** Agents can flag weak or unsourced claims automatically and route them for human review before anything leaves your desk.

content.value:
**60-second reflection:**
Complete this sentence and keep it somewhere visible this week:

“I’ll use **RICECO** to [task] so my outputs are [benefit], and I’ll run **T,R,U,S,T.** to ensure [risk control]. One place I’ll catch errors/lies/hallucinations early is [context].”

**Final thought:**

content.value:
### **From “Who drives?” to “What fuel do they have?”**

In the last module, you learned the three levels of capability: a **chatbot** that passively answers prompts, a **workflow** that follows rails you lay down, and an **agent** that pursues a goal by planning and acting on its own. The big shift was control: from you scripting every step to the model reasoning and acting toward a goal

value: This module answers the next question: regardless of level, **how do you get reliable, on-task outputs?** You have two levers:
**-** **Prompt engineering** (the sprint): craft a clear, structured request for a strong single-turn answer.

**-** **Context (content) engineering** (the marathon): curate what the model can “see” and “use”—documents, tools, prior messages, and memory—so it can reason over trusted sources and act. The accompanying diagram contrasts a minimal input window with a rich, curated context window that includes files, history, and tool calls.

content.value: By the end, you’ll know when a precise prompt is enough and when to layer context (docs, policy PDFs, search/tools, memory) for depth, accuracy, and repeatability; the foundation for agentic work.

sections.title: Video: Why Context Engineering Matters in 6 Minutes

content.value: Great AI work starts with choosing the right lever. **Prompt engineering** gets you crisp, single-turn outputs fast. **Context engineering** builds a reliable “world” around the model. Such as sources, tools, and memory, so it can produce grounded, auditable results for complex tasks. The video walks through when to pick each and how to start with a solid prompt, then layer context as stakes rise

In this short video, we’ll show how a good prompt sets direction, and how context supplies the facts, structure, and guardrails. You’ll see everyday examples (translation, brainstorming) where a single prompt is perfect, and higher-stakes work (briefings, FAQs, policy summaries) where adding context, such as; source PDFs, style rules, memory about audience. Which will dramatically improves accuracy and auditability. Watch for the “ladder up” sequence: start with a clean prompt, then add context in layers as the task hardens.

### **Post Video Short Reflections**
**1) From asking to architecting.** You saw how prompt engineering shines for speed and clarity; give a role, concrete instructions, constraints, and a clear output format to get quality in one turn. Then you contrasted it with context engineering, where you **design the model’s inputs and capabilities** (docs, tools, memory, prior messages) so it can reason over trusted sources and act. The diagram makes that shift visible: minimal inputs vs. a curated context + tool calls

**2) Choosing the right mode**. Use **prompts** for quick drafts, translations, and “answer-once” tasks; use context for research, policy work, analytics, or anything needing repeatability and citations. You don’t have to pick forever: **prototype with a prompt, then layer context** as complexity and risk rise.

This diagram shows the difference between **prompt engineering** and **context (content) engineering** at a glance. On the left, you see the “single-turn” world: a clear prompt goes in, a draft comes out; great for speed and wording. On the right, you see a curated **context window** where the model can also “see” selected documents, prior messages or memory, and even call tools, which is better for depth, accuracy, and repeatable work. Read it left-to-right as a shift from asking well to **architecting the model’s working environment.** Use it to decide when a strong prompt is enough, and when to layer context and tools as complexity and risk rise.

sections.title: Chatbot vs. Workflow vs. Agent - what’s the real difference?

content.value: The terms **chatbot, workflow, and agent** describe how much initiative and real-world capability you give an AI, that choice directly affects speed, reliability, and risk in your day-to-day work. A **chatbot** is great when you need words now: a clear prompt in, a polished draft out (emails, outlines, rewrites), but it won’t check calendars, pull policy sections, or act unless you tell it to. A **workflow** adds tools and guardrails so the system can follow a repeatable path you define; “look up the policy → extract sections → draft a summary → file it here”—perfect for routine tasks that touch live data, though improvements still come from you adjusting the steps. An **agent** is outcome-driven: you give it a goal (“produce a briefing with verified sources”), and it plans, chooses tools, checks its own work, and iterates without you hand-holding each step.

**Knowing which level to use and when** means fewer rewrites, stronger sourcing, clearer accountability, and safer automation. In practice: use a chatbot for rapid drafting, a workflow for consistent, auditable processes, and an agent when you need a system that can think through the path, act across systems, and self-improve under your rules. This section matters because Level 2 will have you move between these levels deliberately, so you can deliver faster with lower risk and designs that scale.

**Bottom line:** the journey from chatbot → workflow → agent is a shift in control. You move from telling a machine how to do something to telling it what outcome to achieve — and letting it figure out the steps.

In this short video, you’ll see how three “levels” of AI capability change what’s possible in your day-to-day work: a **chatbot** that drafts words on command, a **workflow** that follows a tool-connected path you design, and an **agent** that takes a goal and figures out the steps on its own.

value: **Watch for two ideas as you go:**
**(1)** how much initiative the system has (does it only answer, does it follow rails, or does it plan and act?),
**(2)** how that affects speed, reliability, and risk.

content.value: By the end, you should be able to look at any task on your plate and decide: “Is this a quick chatbot job, a repeatable workflow, or something I should hand to an agent with clear guardrails?”

Now that you’ve seen the three levels in action, use them deliberately. Reach for a **chatbot** when you need fast words and you already have the facts. Switch to a **workflow** when the task must touch live systems or follow a repeatable, auditable path you control. Choose an **agent** when you want outcome-oriented automation: give it a goal, the allowed tools and sources, plus verification rules (like **T.R.U.S.T.**), and let it plan, act, and improve. As you continue through Level 2, you’ll mix these levels: start simple with a **chatbot**, codify the reliable steps into a **workflow**, and graduate to an **agent** when the work benefits from autonomous planning and iteration under your governance.

content.value:
### **From Chatbot → Workflow → Agent**

You just walked the arc from “words-on-demand” to “goal-seeking systems.” The core idea to keep: as you move up the levels, you hand over more initiative and real-world capability, shifting from giving instructions to giving outcomes. In the video, Level 1 is a closed-box LLM (great at drafting, passive); Level 2 connects tools on fixed “railroad tracks” (repeatable, auditable, but you’re still the decision-maker); Level 3 promotes the LLM to the decision-maker (it plans, chooses tools, checks itself, and iterates toward the goal).

value: **Key takeaways**
**Level 1: Chatbot/LLM** → Fast drafting, no live/private data, no initiative.
**Level 2: Workflow** → Tools + guardrails; reliable, consistent paths you design.
**Level 3: Agent**→ Goal-driven; reasons, acts, and self-improves under your rules.
**Risk & accountability** increase with capability; choose the level that matches the task, stakes, and compliance needs.
**Quick picker: Which level should I use?**
Need polished wording now (emails, outlines, reframes)? **Use a Chatbot.**
Need a repeatable, auditable process touching live data? **Build a Workflow.**
Need outcome-seeking autonomy across systems (with oversight)? **Deploy an Agent.**
**Apply it (10 minutes)**
**1)** Pick one task you do weekly (e.g., “collect 3 news links → summarize → post draft”).
**2)** Write the workflow steps you’d trust today.
**3)** Circle steps where an agent could (safely) decide/iterate on its own next time.
**4)** Note the guardrails you’d require (sources, approvals, logs).
**Common pitfalls to avoid**
**-** Expecting a chatbot to read calendars or policy repositories.
**-** Over-engineering a workflow for a one-off drafting task.
**-** Giving an agent an ambiguous goal or no verification policy.
**“Good looks like” checklist**
**-** The chosen level matches the **risk, speed, and oversight** you need.
**-** Inputs/outputs are **logged** and **verifiable** (especially for workflows/agents).
**-** There’s a **clear success metric** (what “good” means) and a **fail-safe** (what to do if not met).

content.value:
### **Next Steps: Prompt Engineering vs Context (Content) Engineering**

In the next module, we’ll go deeper on how you get reliable results at any level by separating two skills:

value: **-** **Prompt engineering:** crafting the **ask** (role, instructions, constraints, outputs).

**-** **Context engineering:** shaping the **evidence & environment** the model sees (documents, data retrieval/RAG, tool outputs, examples, policies)—so answers are grounded, auditable, and agent-ready.
**Why this matters for agents:**
**-** Agents succeed or fail on the **goal clarity** (prompt) and the **quality/structure of the information & tools** they can access (context).
**-** Strong prompt + strong context = fewer rewrites, safer automation, and agents that can **reason, act, and self-check** against the right sources.
When you’re ready, jump to **Prompting vs Context Engineering** module to continue your agent creation journey!

sections.title: Introduction to Generative AI: A 2025 Perspective

content.value: Welcome to the introductory class on Generative AI, presented by Deputy Minister Janak Alford. This module provides a foundational understanding of Generative AI as it stands in 2025, focusing on its application in accelerating business. We'll explore the core concepts, frameworks, and technologies that are shaping the future of AI.

Generative AI, unlike traditional AI which focuses on prediction or classification, is about *creation*. It allows machines to generate new content, be it text, images, audio, or even code. In 2025, Generative AI is no longer a novelty; it's a crucial tool for innovation and efficiency.

sections.title: Mental Models for Approaching Generative AI

content.value: To effectively utilize Generative AI, it's crucial to adopt specific mental models. These models help us understand the capabilities and limitations of the technology, enabling us to apply it strategically.

value: **The 'AI as a Partner' Model:** View AI not as a replacement for human labor, but as a collaborative partner that augments human capabilities.
**The 'Experimentation-Driven' Model:** Embrace a culture of experimentation, recognizing that the best applications of Generative AI often emerge from iterative testing and refinement.
**The 'Ethical Considerations' Model:** Prioritize ethical considerations, ensuring that AI is used responsibly and does not perpetuate bias or harm.

data.name: 1.6.3 AI Research Tools: Capabilities and Use in the Public Sector

json_data.title: 1.6.3 AI Research Tools: Capabilities and Use in the Public Sector

content.value: The purpose of this module is to introduce commonly used AI research tools, explain what they are designed to do, and clarify how they can be used responsibly to support wide and deep research in the public sector.
This module focuses on:

value: Understanding tool capabilities at a high level
Knowing when a tool is appropriate to use
Recognizing limitations and risks
Reinforcing human accountability for research outcomes

sections.title: AI Research Tools: What They Are

content.value: AI research tools are software systems designed to **assist humans in conducting research tasks** by leveraging large language models and related AI capabilities. Their primary role is to **augment human analytical capacity**, not to replace professional judgment, accountability, or decision-making.

At a practical level, AI research tools help users work more efficiently with information by accelerating activities that are typically time-intensive, repetitive, or cognitively demanding. These tools operate across multiple stages of the research process, from early exploration to structured analysis and drafting.
**What AI Research Tools Do**
AI research tools commonly support activities such as:

value: Identifying relevant information across large or unfamiliar domains
Summarizing and organizing complex or lengthy material
Comparing approaches, options, or perspectives
Structuring research outputs into coherent formats
Assisting with drafting, refinement, and iteration

content.value: They are particularly effective when the volume of information is high, timelines are constrained, or consistency across outputs is important.

sections.title: How AI Research Tools Fit Into the Research Process

content.value: AI research tools can be used at different points in the research lifecycle:

value: **Early-stage research:** supporting wide research by accelerating scanning, summarization, and landscape mapping
**Mid-stage research:** helping structure analysis, compare options, and organize findings
**Late-stage research:** assisting with drafting briefs, synthesizing insights, and improving clarity and consistency

content.value: At each stage, the quality of outputs depends heavily on:

value: The clarity of the research question
The quality of inputs and sources
The judgment applied by the human user

content.value: No single tool is best for all research tasks.

value: **Wide research** benefits from tools optimized for breadth and synthesis
**Deep research** benefits from tools that support structured reasoning and evidence testing
**Decision-grade research** always requires human judgment, regardless of tool

sections.title: Gemini Deep Research (up to Protected A)

content.value: **Gemini Deep Research** is a research-oriented capability designed to perform broad, multi-step exploration across a topic. It emphasizes synthesis across sources and structured summaries.

In practice, it functions as a powerful accelerator for early-stage research, where the primary goal is to understand what exists, how an issue is being approached elsewhere, and what themes or patterns are emerging.

In a public-sector context, Gemini Deep Research is most useful when an issue is unfamiliar, evolving, or requires a broad scan across jurisdictions, sectors, or disciplines. It can assist with horizon scanning, jurisdictional reviews, and early framing by quickly producing overviews that would otherwise take significant time to assemble manually. However, its outputs should be treated as provisional. While it can surface themes and summarize material effectively, conclusions drawn from its outputs must be validated, contextualized, and refined through deeper analysis and human judgment before being used to inform decisions.

sections.title: Copilot Researcher Agent (up to Protected B)

content.value: The **Copilot Researcher Agent** is an advanced research-oriented AI assistant available within Microsoft 365 Copilot. It is specifically designed to handle complex, multi-step research tasks by gathering information from both the web and the user’s own work content — including files, emails, meetings, and chats that the user has permission to access.

Unlike the standard Copilot experience, which answers simple questions and provides quick summaries, the Researcher Agent is built to take longer, think deeper, and produce structured, source-cited reports. It deliberately performs more thoughtful analysis by integrating information from multiple sources and organizing it into a coherent, decision-oriented output.

Because it pulls from both internal data (such as documents stored in Microsoft 365) and external web content, the Copilot Researcher Agent can blend contextual knowledge of organizational materials with up-to-date external information, making its outputs more relevant for work-specific research tasks.

In essence, this agent acts as a supercharged research partner that goes beyond surface-level summarization. It is designed to help users work more efficiently by collecting evidence, organizing findings, and presenting them in a structured format that supports analysis and decision making.

While powerful, it does not replace human oversight. It still depends on the user to define research questions clearly, judge the relevance and reliability of sources, and decide how to interpret and apply the information it produces.

Manus is an autonomous artificial intelligence agent. It is designed to perform complex, multi-step tasks across a variety of domains with minimal continuous human supervision by planning and executing workflows independently. Unlike traditional chat-oriented AI tools that respond to individual prompts, Manus has been built to accept high-level objectives and carry them through to substantial results by breaking them down into actionable steps, integrating with external tools and data sources, and producing structured outcomes like reports, analyses, and other deliverables.

Manus’s architecture enables **autonomous task execution** in the cloud, meaning that once a user defines a task, the agent can continue working on it in the background without requiring constant direction. This includes activities such as gathering information from multiple sources, analyzing datasets, synthesizing findings into organized formats, and generating outputs like summaries, tables, visualizations, or even code. Its design supports asynchronous operation, which allows users to proceed with other work while Manus completes assigned research or analytical tasks.

A distinctive aspect of Manus is its focus on **workflow automation and execution**. Rather than simply providing conversational responses, it integrates planning, execution, and synthesis, making it appropriate for applications that involve extended sequences of actions or require outputs beyond simple text. This includes capabilities often associated with research tasks particularly when those tasks involve synthesizing information across web sources, internal data, and complex analytical objectives.

data.name: 1.1.4 - Meet Albert
data.description: This module will introduce you to Albert, an advanced AI assistant platform from the Government of Alberta. You will learn what Albert is, what it can do, and how to get started using Albert.

json_data.title: 1.1.4 - Meet Albert

content.value:
**Albert is a free and secure AI assistant** designed to help you with a wide range of tasks.
Whether you need to get quick answers, automate complex workflows, or analyze data,
Albert provides the tools to make it happen. Developed with a focus on security and
privacy, Albert is **a trusted platform for all Albertans.** 

 

**Note:** At this time, Albert is approved for use with Public data only. Please do not share personal, confidential, or highly sensitive content in Albert.

value: **Getting Started**

content.value:
Getting started with Albert is easy. Follow these simple steps to create your account and
begin exploring the platform.
**Creating Your Account**

value: **• Visit the Albert website:** Open your web browser and go to the Albert homepage here: [Albert Platform Homepage](https://albert.it.com/)
**• Start the registration process:** Click on the **"Create Free Account"** button.
**• Fill in your details:** You will be taken to a sign-up page where you will need to provide your email address and create a password.

content.value: **Signing In**

value: **• Signing In:** Once you have created your account, you can sign in to Albert at any time.
**• Go to the Sign In page:** Click on the **"Sign In"** button on the homepage.
**• Enter your credentials:** Type in your email address and password, then click **"Sign In"**.
**Next:** Exploring the Albert Platform

content.value:
Once you log in, you will be greeted by the main Albert interface. You may also be presented
with a welcome tour that introduces the platform's key features.
The platform is organized into several key areas, each designed for a specific set of tasks.
Let's take a look at the core features of Albert.

value: **Core Features**

content.value:
Albert offers a suite of powerful features to help you with your tasks. Here’s a closer look
at each one.

value: **Chat: Your Conversational AI**

content.value: The Chat feature is your primary way to interact with Albert. You can ask questions, generate images, upload files for analysis, share conversations, get information, brainstorm ideas, and chat with specialized agents - all in a natural, conversational way.

value: **How to use the Chat feature:** Visit: [Albert Main Chat](https://albert.it.com/chat/)
**• 1 Start a new chat:** Click on the **"New Chat"** button in the sidebar.
**• 2 Type your message:** Enter your question or prompt in the text box at the bottom of the screen.
**• 3 Get a response:** Albert will provide a detailed response to your query.
**Agents: Create Custom AI Assistants**

content.value:
The Agents feature allows you to build specialized AI assistants for specific tasks. You can
create agents from scratch or use pre-built templates to get started quickly.

value: **How to use the Agents feature:** Visit: [Albert Agents](https://albert.it.com/agents/)
**• 1 Navigate to Agents:** Click on the **"Agents"** tab in the top navigation bar.
**• 2 Create a new agent:** Click on the **"Create Agent"** button.
**• 3 Configure your agent:** Define the agent's purpose, skills, and knowledge base.
**Stage: Build Workflows in Stages**

content.value: The Stage feature provides a simple way to create multi-step workflows. You can chain together different agents and functions to automate a series of tasks that are executed in stages.

value: **How to use the Stage feature:** Visit [Albert Stage](https://albert.it.com/stage/)
**• 1 Go to Stage:** Click on the **"Stage"** tab in the navigation bar.
**• 2 Add a stage:** Click **"Add Stage"** to create a new step in your workflow.
**• 3 Configure the stage:** Select an agent or function for the stage and provide the necessary inputs.
**Canvas: Visualize Your Workflows**

content.value: The Canvas feature provides a powerful visual editor for designing complex workflows. You can add nodes (such as inputs, agents, and functions) and connect them to build sophisticated automation pipelines.

value: **How to use the Canvas feature:** Visit: [Albert Canvas](https://albert.it.com/canvas/)
**• 1 Open the Canvas:** Click on the **"Canvas"** tab.
**• 2 Add nodes:** Select nodes from the sidebar to add them to the canvas.
**• 3 Connect the nodes:** Draw connections between the nodes to define the flow of your workflow.
**Image Analysis: Understand Your Visuals**

content.value:
With the Image Analysis feature, you can upload images and have Albert analyze them for
you. This is useful for tasks like extracting text from a picture, identifying objects, or getting
a description of what’s in an image.

value: **How to use the Image Analysis feature:** Visit: [Albert Image Analysis](https://albert.it.com/image/)
**• 1 Go to Image:** Click on the **"Image"** tab.
**• 2 Upload an image:** Drag and drop an image file or click to browse your files.
**• 3 Analyze the image:** Add an agent or a custom prompt to analyze an image. Select the image(s) you want to analyze, and ALBERT will provide the results.
**Voice Processing: From Speech to Text and Back**

content.value:
The Voice feature allows you to work with audio. You can convert spoken words into written
text (speech-to-text) or turn written text into spoken words (text-to-speech).

value: **How to use the Voice Processing feature:** Visit: [Albert Voice Processing](https://albert.it.com/voice/)
**• 1 Navigate to Voice:** Click on the **"Voice"** tab.
**• 2 Choose your tool:** Select either **"Speech to Text"** or **"Text to Speech"**.
**• 3 Speech to Text:** Upload or record audio. Albert will generate a transcription and can detect different speakers.
**• 4 Text to Speech:** Enter text to convert it into speech, and select from various voices for Albert to play back.
**Meeting Transcripts: Analyze Your Meetings**

content.value:
The Transcripts feature is designed to help you make sense of your meeting recordings. You
can upload transcripts from Microsoft Teams and use Albert to summarize them, identify
key points, and extract action items.

value: **How to use the Transcripts feature:** Visit: [Albert Transcript Analysis](https://albert.it.com/transcripts/)
**• 1 Go to Transcripts:** Click on the **"Transcripts"** tab
**• 2 Upload a transcript:** Drag and drop your transcript file (VTT, DOCX, or TXT).
**• 3 Analyze the transcript:** Albert will help you analyze the content of your meeting.
**Prompt Library: Save and Share Your Best Prompts**

content.value:
The Prompt Library is a place where you can store, organize, and share your most effective
prompts. This helps you maintain consistency in your AI interactions and collaborate with
others.

value: **How to use the Prompt Library:** Visit: [Albert Prompt Library](https://albert.it.com/prompts/)
**• 1 Access the library:** Click on the Prompt Library icon in the toolbar.
**• 2 Create a new prompt:** Click **"New Prompt"** to configure and save a prompt.
**• 3 Browse and use prompts:** Search through your saved prompts or explore the marketplace for prompts shared by others.
**Next:** Additional Tools and Settings

content.value: Albert offers several **additional tools and settings** to enhance your experience, such as:

value: **Framework Library:** Access pre-built frameworks for common tasks and workflows
**Documentation & Training:** Learn more about Albert through built-in documentation and training materials
**Accessibility Preferences:** Customize the platform to meet your accessibility needs
**Language Toggle:** Switch between English and French (Français)
**Theme Toggle:** Choose between light and dark mode for comfortable viewing
**AI Helper:** Get instant help and answers about using the Albert platform
**Feedback:** Share your thoughts and suggestions to help improve Albert
**Next:** Tips for Getting the Most Out of Albert

sections.title: Tips for Getting the Most Out of Albert

value: Here are some tips to help you make the most of the Albert platform:
**1. Start with Chat:** If you're new to Albert, begin by using the Chat feature to get comfortable with how the AI responds to your questions.
**2. Explore the Templates:** When creating agents or workflows, take advantage of the prebuilt templates to save time.
**3. Use the Prompt Library:** Save your best prompts so you can reuse them later and share them with your team.
**4. Experiment with Workflows:** Try building simple workflows in Stage before moving on to the more complex Canvas interface.
**5. Take the Tour:** If you're unsure about a feature, don't skip the welcome tour—it provides helpful context and guidance.
**Getting Help**

content.value: If you need assistance while using Albert, you have several options:

value: **• AI Helper:** Click on the AI Helper icon on the top left to ask questions about the platform.
**• Documentation & Training:** Access the built-in documentation for detailed guides and tutorials. [Albert User Manual](https://albert.it.com/docs/)
**• Feedback:** Use the feedback feature on the top left to report issues or request new features.
**Security and Privacy**

Your **security and privacy are top priorities** for Albert. The platform is built with enterprise grade
security measures and follows privacy-first principles. **Your data is protected and
remains confidential** while you use the platform.

content.value:
This module introduces agentic workflows, a structured and systematic approach to using AI for complex tasks. Unlike single prompts or one-off AI interactions, agentic workflows break work into a series of deliberate reasoning steps. Each step aligns with how humans naturally process information — perceiving, analyzing, deciding, generating, communicating, and evaluating.

 

By learning this approach, you will understand how complex tasks can be standardized and improved through structured AI support. You will also explore why this approach is more reliable than unstructured prompting and how it enhances quality, consistency, and transparency.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
• Explain what an agentic workflow is
• Identify when a workflow is needed
• Apply the six reasoning blocks to structure work
• Recognize how workflows transform messy inputs into high-quality outputs
• Begin designing workflows that support your team’s processes

 

This module is ultimately about **structuring thinking** so AI can follow it in a predictable and repeatable way.

An agentic workflow is a sequence of AI agents, where each agent is responsible for a specific cognitive role, and holistically they work towards a goal. Instead of asking one AI prompt to handle all aspects of a complex task, the workflow breaks the task into smaller, defined stages. Each stage performs a unique reasoning function and passes its output to the next stage in the sequence.

 

This design achieves several important effects:
• It mirrors how high-performing teams coordinate work: each person (or agent) owns a single part of the process.
• It ensures that AI does not attempt to mix unrelated cognitive tasks at once (e.g., analyzing while generating).
• It creates a logical and predictable flow that moves from **raw input → insight → structured results → polished deliverables.**

 

By thinking of agentic workflows as an “AI relay team,” you can see how structured coordination produces more consistent and reliable outcomes than a single agent trying to do everything simultaneously.

### **1) Education Planner for K–6**

Creates a comprehensive educational lesson plan for Grades K–6 by conducting Google searches on a specified topic, extracting relevant website content, and transforming the research into age-appropriate learning modules that include activities and tutoring materials.

 

### **2) Research to Minister Briefing 1a and 1b**

Generates a formal ministerial briefing note by performing a Google search on a user-defined topic, scraping relevant websites, synthesizing the findings, and formatting the information into a structured, decision-ready document using a standardized briefing template.

 

### **3) Search and Summarize**

Performs Google searches and web scraping on any user-specified topic to collect, organize, and synthesize publicly available information into a concise summary or briefing document.

 

### **4) Deputy Minister Briefing Review**

Reviews and critiques briefing notes, producing a clear, written response to the originator outlining the revisions required. The agent uses examples from the original briefing to illustrate deficiencies and recommend improvements.

 

### **5) Iterative App Ideas**

Develops innovative application ideas based on a specified request, then critiques them for feasibility and security considerations. 
It prepares a proposal for executives that presents up to three options with pros and cons, and also creates a **Lovable application definition** for the top app idea — which can be copied directly into *Lovable* to generate a mockup.

 

### **6) Minister Mission Builder**

Creates an agenda, travel plan, and event speaking notes for engagements related to the Minister of Technology and Innovation. 
The content focuses on areas such as AI, data centres, digital sovereignty, privacy, deepfake protection, and cybersecurity. It also generates a draft travel approval email.

 

### **7) Meeting Transcript to Charter**

Transforms a project meeting transcript into the following structured outputs:  
i - A **Draft Project Charter**  
ii - An **Executive Summary** of the project  
iii - A **Functional Requirements Document** containing questions for stakeholder input  

The agent then conducts both internal and web-based searches to identify existing services that could meet the outlined requirements and produces:  
iv - An **Options Paper** with pros and cons, prioritizing in-house services.

 

It also **stores versioned copies of each artefact**, enabling **future lessons-learned analysis** to identify improvements and **enhance the overall workflow**.

data.name: 1.6 Foundations of AI Research in the Public Sector
data.description:
The purpose of this module is to establish a shared, practical understanding of AI research: what it is, what it is not, and how it is responsibly applied in the public sector.

This module clarifies how AI-enabled research supports evidence-informed decision-making, improves the speed and quality of analysis, and reduces uncertainty in complex policy, program, and operational contexts. It distinguishes rigorous research from information gathering, explains the unique constraints of public-sector environments, and sets expectations for defensibility, transparency, and accountability when using AI tools.

json_data.title: 1.6 Foundations of AI Research in the Public Sector

content.value: Research is the disciplined process of reducing uncertainty in order to support decisions. It is **the structured collection, evaluation, synthesis, and interpretation of information to generate reliable insight under uncertainty**.
Research performs a **small number of critical functions**. When any of these are missing or weak, the quality of decisions degrades.

**Framing** defines the real question being answered. It clarifies what decision the research is meant to support and ensures effort is not spent solving the wrong problem. Poor framing leads to technically sound work that is strategically useless.

**Scanning** identifies what exists across relevant domains, jurisdictions, evidence bases, and perspectives. Its purpose is to reduce blind spots and avoid false novelty. Without adequate scanning, decisions are made with incomplete awareness of options and risks.

**Filtering** separates signal from noise. It prioritizes what is relevant, credible, and impactful given the decision context. This function prevents overload, false equivalence, and wasted attention on low-value information.

**Validation** tests claims, sources, and assumptions. It asks whether evidence is reliable, comparable, and applicable to the public-sector context. This function directly reduces decision risk and prevents overconfidence.

**Synthesis** integrates findings into coherent insight. It connects evidence to implications, trade-offs, and recommended actions. Without synthesis, research remains descriptive and does not enable decision-making.
1. Exploratory Research

Goal: Understand the space

Used when: problem is ill-defined

Output: maps, themes, questions
Analytical Research

Goal: Explain relationships

Used when: trade-offs exist

Output: comparisons, causal logic
Evaluative Research

Goal: Judge effectiveness

Used when: programs or policies exist

Output: performance insights, gaps
Decision-Support Research

Goal: Enable a choice

User when: stakes are high

Output: recommendations with risk framing

Public-sector research operates in an environment that is **fundamentally different from private-sector or academic research**. Understanding this context is essential to using AI responsibly and effectively.
**Structural context**

Public-sector research is shaped by legislative mandates, political timelines, and accountability requirements. Decisions often need to balance evidence, public interest, legal constraints, and stakeholder considerations simultaneously. As a result, research must be timely, defensible, and aligned with governance processes.
**Information environment**

Government research draws from a wide range of sources, including administrative data, jurisdictional comparisons, academic studies, stakeholder input, and internal reporting. These sources are often distributed across systems, vary in quality and format, and evolve over time. Research must therefore reconcile incomplete, imperfect, or non-standardized information.
**Human and organizational realities**

Public servants conducting research are typically generalists working across multiple files, often under time pressure. Research must be produced collaboratively, reviewed by multiple levels, and communicated clearly to non-technical decision-makers. Consistency, clarity, and traceability matter as much as analytical depth.
**Risk and accountability considerations**

Unlike many other sectors, public-sector research must withstand public scrutiny, access-to-information requests, audits, and retrospective review. This creates a strong emphasis on transparency, documentation, and defensibility in how research is conducted and presented.

Taken together, these conditions mean that public-sector research prioritizes reliability, clarity, and trustworthiness over speed or novelty alone. Any use of AI in research must respect and strengthen these priorities, not undermine them.

json_data.title: 2.1.3 Thinking Like AI

content.value: This module walks through a framework and approach to engage AI so you can get more meaningful interactions and build effective agents and agentic workflows.

## **Analogy: The Warehouse Mind of Artificial Intelligence**

Imagine, for a moment, that you are an artificial intelligence model situated within a vast, empty warehouse.

 

During training, information begins to arrive — various objects such as fruit, animals, and toys — and your task is to organize and categorize them based on observed similarities and relationships.

 

- You notice that fruit tends to occupy one section, and within that, red fruit such as apples and cherries cluster more closely together than yellow fruit such as bananas.  
- Similarly, toy animals form their own clusters — elephants and giraffes are positioned near each other, while rabbits and mice form another group within a separate zone.

 

Over time, the warehouse transforms into a structured map of meaning, where related concepts exist in close proximity.

 

This organizational system represents what are known as **embeddings** — the model’s internal method of mapping meaning within a multi-dimensional space.  
Each item’s position corresponds to a **vector**, which serves as a set of coordinates describing how strongly it relates to other items.

 

Now, imagine a person enters the warehouse and provides a prompt:

> “I’m looking for fruit.”

You respond:

> “Certainly — proceed forward approximately ten steps.”

When the person adds:

> “Red fruit.”

You refine your response:

> “Turn left a few steps — you are likely seeking an apple.”

 

It arrives at this conclusion because it has encountered similar patterns during training and recognizes the association between *red fruit* and *apple*.  
This sequence reflects the predictive process at work:

**Prompt → Embeddings (meaning + sequence = context) → Highest-probability next vector = Next word (response).**

 

---

## **When Things Go Wrong (Hallucinations)**

Occasionally, the system receives insufficient context. For instance, someone might enter and say:

> “I want red.”

At this point, the model hesitates.  
Red *what* — fruit, toy, or vehicle?

It generates a guess, perhaps:

> “Red ball?”

When the user replies, “No, that’s incorrect,” the model has experienced a **hallucination** — an inaccurate prediction produced due to missing or ambiguous context.

 

---

## **Adding Structure (RICECO)**

To address this challenge, designers introduce a structured approach to gathering user intent.  
They create a form with sections for **Role**, **Inputs**, **Context**, **Examples**, **Criteria**, and **Output** — collectively known as **RICECO**.

 

Each time the form is completed, the model receives clearer information about the user’s goals, the provided inputs, and the desired outputs.  
As a result, its predictions become far more accurate — fewer assumptions, more relevant responses.

 

---

## **Scaling Up (Large Models)**

Now, imagine the single warehouse expanding into a massive, coordinated operation — similar to a large distribution centre with thousands of specialized workers collaborating to fulfill complex requests.

 

This represents the evolution to a **large language model (LLM)** — the same underlying principles of pattern recognition and organization, scaled exponentially.  
More workers equate to more knowledge, richer connections, and greater contextual understanding — resulting in higher accuracy and faster responses.

 

Ultimately, this progression reflects the shift from a single model making educated guesses to a collective system capable of reasoning and delivering with precision.  
The **key takeaway** is that our goal when working with AI is to **narrow its probability space** — to reduce uncertainty in its predictions.  
Structure helps transform AI’s “best guess” into a more reliable and contextually grounded response.

 

---

## **Analogy: The Human Warehouse**

Now, consider the reverse scenario — you are the one standing in the warehouse.

 

Unlike the AI, you are not surrounded merely by objects. You possess **senses**, **memories**, and **emotions**.  
You can **see**, **hear**, **feel**, and even infer meaning beyond what is explicitly stated.

 

Someone enters and says:

> “I want red.”

Rather than pausing in confusion, you observe their facial expression, tone of voice, and body language.  
You recall that earlier they were looking at fruit and respond:

> “Do you mean a red apple?”

They nod in confirmation.

 

This illustrates the human advantage — **cognition**.  
You draw upon empathy, perception, and experience to interpret incomplete information and derive intent before words are even finished.

 

The human reasoning process can be expressed as follows:

**Prompt → Cognition (senses + empathy + experience + intuition + intent = understanding) → Contextual reasoning = Response or action.**

 

While the AI searches the warehouse for patterns, you examine the **person** for context.  
You do not calculate probabilities; instead, you make **judgments** informed by experience and emotion.

 

That is why **humans excel at nuance**, whereas **AI excels at structure**.

 

---

## **Bridging the Two**

When collaborating with AI, we are effectively connecting these two worlds.  
The key lies in **translating human understanding into structured context** — providing the AI with the clarity it requires to reason as we intend.

 

This concept is illustrated in the diagram, which shows that different forms of input to AI possess varying degrees of structure — with formats such as **JSON** being highly structured and therefore more easily interpreted by AI systems.

## **Systems Composition and Alignment with AI**

This diagram on the left illustrates how **systems are composed**.

 

At the foundation, we begin with **tasks** — individual actions performed in isolation.
**Processes** are sequences of tasks connected by defined inputs and outputs.
When multiple processes are linked together, they form a **workflow**.  
When those workflows are integrated and include **feedback** and **continuous improvement mechanisms**, they evolve into a **system**.
At the highest level, **ecosystems** emerge — networks of multiple systems that interact, adapt, and evolve together.

 

You can also view this as a reflection of an organization:  
from **individuals** performing their tasks,  
to **teams**, **departments**, and entire **networks** working collectively toward shared goals.

 

---

On the right, the diagram shows how **artificial intelligence aligns with systems thinking**.

 

While the alignment is not always one-to-one, it can be generally understood as follows:

- **AI Assistants** (such as Copilot or ChatGPT) operate at the **task** level.  
- **AI Agents** function at the **process** level.  
- **Agentic workflows** correspond to **systems**, integrating multiple steps with feedback loops.  
- **AI orchestration** represents **ecosystems**, where multiple intelligent agents and humans collaborate toward shared organizational objectives.

## **Applying Systems Thinking**

 

**First**, look beyond individual tasks.  
Do not only ask, “What am I doing?” — instead, consider, “How does what I’m doing affect the next step or the next person?”  
**Systems thinking** is about recognizing those interdependencies and understanding how actions influence the broader flow of work.

 

**Second**, identify the key **inputs**, **outputs**, and **feedback loops** that drive the system’s behavior.  
Ask yourself: *What comes in, what goes out, and how does feedback reshape the process over time?*  
That is how systems learn, adapt, and improve.

 

**Third**, focus on **patterns rather than steps**.  
Instead of designing for isolated exceptions, design for what repeats.  
If something occurs frequently, it likely represents an underlying system — and that is where the most meaningful improvements can be made.

 

**Fourth**, **connect across boundaries**.  
Most challenges do not reside neatly within a single team — they exist in the spaces between them.  
Recognizing these connections helps identify where information becomes stalled, duplicated, or misaligned.

 

**Finally**, **align everything to the system’s goal**.  
Every component — whether a person, process, or tool — should contribute toward a **shared outcome**.  
This alignment ensures that systems remain coherent and that the organization moves forward collectively, rather than in separate or competing directions.

The **F.O.C.U.S. Framework** is a simple and practical method for **structuring your work before engaging with AI**.  
It helps ensure that your prompts, context, and expectations are clearly defined — allowing AI to collaborate effectively and deliver meaningful results.

 

**F — Frame the Problem**  
Begin by clearly defining the **goal or challenge** you are addressing.  
Ask yourself: *What do I actually need help with, and why does it matter?*  
Clarity at this stage ensures the AI focuses on solving the right problem.

 

**O — Opportunity for AI**  
Determine **where AI can add value**.  
Perhaps it can enhance **speed**, **accuracy**, or **pattern recognition** — helping you see insights that might otherwise remain hidden.

 

**C — Context and Content**  
Define the **environment** in which the AI will operate and what **information** it can safely access or rely upon.  
The richer and more accurate the context, the more relevant and precise the AI’s responses will be.

 

**U — User Intent and Instructions**  
Specify your **intent** and provide clear **instructions** for the AI.  
This is where the **RICECO framework** supports you — outlining the AI’s **role**, the **inputs**, and the **expected behaviour** during the task.

 

**S — Structure the Output**  
Set expectations for **what success looks like**.  
Whether the output is a **summary**, a **table**, or a **short draft**, defining the desired format ensures the AI delivers something **useful and aligned** the first time.

## **Bringing It All Together**

Now we bring everything together — **thinking like AI**, **systems thinking**, and the **F.O.C.U.S. Framework** —  
and apply these concepts to a **worked example**.

 

This integration demonstrates how structured thinking, contextual awareness, and clear framing combine to create more effective **AI-enabled workflows** and **decision-making processes**.

## **Expected Outcomes of the Reimagined Workflow**

What are the **expected outcomes** of the reimagined workflow?

 

**First — Time Reduction**  
By minimizing duplication and automating repetitive tasks, the process achieves **up to 80% less manual effort**.

 

**Second — Increased Throughput**  
Teams are able to complete **two to three times more reviews** within the same timeframe, significantly improving operational efficiency.

 

**Third — Traceability and Accountability**  
Every **action** and **decision** within the workflow is **recorded**, **verifiable**, and **auditable**, ensuring transparency and maintaining trust across all stakeholders.

## **Recap**

By understanding **how AI works**, applying **systems thinking**, and using the **F.O.C.U.S. Framework**,  
we enable ourselves to **design and build effective agents and intelligent workflows**.

 

This combination of **structured reasoning**, **contextual awareness**, and **intentional design** allows AI to operate in alignment with our goals —  
enhancing efficiency, consistency, and the overall quality of outcomes.
